architecture.job: Turn images and proprioception into a [16,10] chunk, and decide when a chunk is stale.
architecture.interface: In: camera frames + joint state. Out: [16,10] float array + the anchor pose it was taken against.
architecture.size: 0 new lines if you use a library policy; dummy_policy.py (224 lines) is your stand-in and is the right move for now. Camera path is currently 0 lines.
architecture.note: Their H=16 at dt=0.04 is 0.64 s of open loop, SHORTER than every library default (ACT 3.3 s, pi0 1.0 s). Defensible, but inference must finish in well under 0.64 s or the queue starves.

architecture.layer: Chunk semantics + decode (6D rot, anchor, 5-DOF projection, gripper width)
architecture.job: Gram-Schmidt 6D -> R, compose T_anchor @ dT, drop the yaw the mechanism forces, map width to a gripper angle.
architecture.interface: In: [16,10] + anchor T. Out: 16 x (5 joint angles + gripper angle).
architecture.size: action_format.py, 192 lines. Zero ROS, zero SDK. Moves to a direct driver untouched.
architecture.note: Take the anchor ONCE when the chunk arrives and expand all 16 steps to absolute immediately. Re-anchoring per tick is the drift bug LeRobot's synchronous engine refuses to run relative policies because of.

architecture.job: EE pose <-> joint1..joint5, with EE yaw forced to atan2(y, x - BASE_X).
architecture.interface: In: 4x4 pose. Out: 5 joints, or a refusal.
architecture.size: omx_kinematics.py, 216 lines, imports only math. Re-validated: 17,200/20,000 exact at worst error 3.24e-16 m, 2,800 refusals, zero wrong answers.
architecture.note: All 2,800 refusals are negative-planar-reach poses (arm folded behind its own joint1 axis); restricted to r >= 0 it is 13,887/13,887. Their working envelope is entirely inside the exact region. The CODE survives the migration; its CALIBRATION does not.

architecture.job: Hold the newest chunk, know how far wall-clock has advanced into it, splice a new chunk in without a discontinuity.
architecture.interface: In: chunk + arrival time. Out: 'which two steps am I between, and what fraction'.
architecture.size: ~30 lines of real logic exist inside chunk_executor_node.py; a standalone buffer with late-chunk and splice handling is 60-90 lines.
architecture.note: PUBLISH_STEPS=8 exists ONLY because JointTrajectoryController rejects a trajectory ending in nonzero velocity. Owning the loop deletes that constraint entirely and collapses the publish-ahead dance into 'keep the buffer two chunks deep'. Biggest single simplification the rewrite buys.

architecture.layer: Command gate: limits, rate, workspace, IK-failure
architecture.job: Refuse NaN and non-orthonormal rotations, clamp each joint to a measured limit, reject a step whose implied joint speed the servo cannot deliver, and keep the EE above the table.
architecture.interface: In: 16 joint vectors. Out: the same, or a rejection that holds position.
architecture.size: ~120-200 lines. They have ~18 (the MAX_JOINT_VEL gate). This is the layer that replaces everything ros2_control silently enforced.
architecture.note: Their MAX_JOINT_VEL = 180 deg/s = 3.14 rad/s may never fire before the firmware clamps first — see the profile-semantics disagreement. The table matters more than self-collision: 6.48 mm droop turns a commanded z=+5 mm into a real z=-1.5 mm.

architecture.job: Bridge 25 Hz chunk steps to whatever rate the bus runs.
architecture.interface: In: waypoints + times. Out: one goal position per loop tick.
architecture.size: ~40 lines for a cubic Hermite (the central-difference velocities already exist in build_segment), or 0 lines if you let the servo's own profile generator do it.
architecture.note: Position-servo projects (LeRobot, ALOHA) do not interpolate in software — LeRobot's interpolator is 136 lines and OFF by default. UMI builds a 990-line interpolator because it has a 12.5x rate gap; at 25 Hz into a 50 ms servo profile, they do not.

architecture.job: Wake on a deadline, sample, write the bus, read state back, never drift, and freeze if no chunk arrives.
architecture.interface: In: the buffer. Out: one sync_write + one sync_read per tick.
architecture.size: ~20 lines for the loop, ~15 for the instrumentation. Write both on day one.
architecture.note: next_deadline += period, then sleep(next_deadline - now). Never sleep(period). Never print() inside the loop — 0.05-5 ms, larger than everything else combined, and the usual reason people conclude 'Python is too slow'.

architecture.job: theta = (tick - tick_zero) * 2*pi/4096 * sign, per joint, measured not assumed.
architecture.interface: In: 6 raw ticks. Out: 6 radians in the frame omx_kinematics expects.
architecture.size: ~40 lines of code, 3-6 hours at the bench with torque off. The measurement is the work, not the code.
architecture.note: This is the actual blocker and everything above it is already written and waiting. Every number in dummy_exec is in the vendor's joint frame — offsets already applied by code they cannot read. Read Homing Offset (addr 20) first: if it is nonzero, the CENTER=2048 hypothesis in s2_read.py is wrong by exactly that much and the 'mystery mapping' is just one register.

architecture.job: On every connect: verify models and firmware, torque off, write EEPROM, read it back, write RAM, read it back, Goal := Present, torque on.
architecture.interface: In: a config table in git. Out: six servos in a known, asserted state.
architecture.size: ~250-350 lines including the readback-and-diff, which is the half everyone skips and the half that earns its keep. 1-2 days.
architecture.note: The RAM/EEPROM boundary is address 64. Operating Mode, Drive Mode, Return Delay Time and position limits PERSIST; P/I/D gains, Profile Velocity and Profile Acceleration DO NOT. That single fact is the complete explanation of their 'registers silently resetting' mystery.

architecture.layer: Fault detection and recovery state machine
architecture.job: Watch the Alert bit in every status packet, read Hardware Error Status (70), Reboot (0x08) to clear, then replay the ENTIRE RAM init for that servo.
architecture.interface: In: status-packet error byte. Out: a recovered, reconfigured servo, or a hard stop.
architecture.size: ~150-200 lines. Cost is provoking each fault deliberately, not the code.
architecture.note: Recovery is not 're-enable torque'. On X-series the only exit from a latched Shutdown is Reboot, which wipes RAM back to defaults — so an overload at 3 a.m. silently reverts that joint to Kp=640 and Profile Velocity=0 mid-run with no power cycle to blame.

architecture.layer: Failsafe: Bus Watchdog, torque ordering, shutdown mask
architecture.job: Decide what the arm does when your Python dies, and make the servo enforce it without you.
architecture.interface: In: register 98 (20 ms units) and the torque sequence. Out: freeze-in-place instead of drop or slam.
architecture.size: ~80 lines, but a full day because it is almost all kill -9 and cable-yank testing.
architecture.note: Bus Watchdog stops motion and makes goal registers read-only but does NOT clear Torque Enable — the arm freezes rather than collapses, which is correct for an arm that already droops. Corollary: a power-cutting e-stop is a WORSE safety device here than the watchdog, because cutting power IS the drop.

architecture.job: Six goal positions in one packet, six present positions in one request.
architecture.interface: In: 6 tick values. Out: 6 tick values, correctly attributed by ID.
architecture.size: ~100-150 lines. This is the single concrete gap in dxl_raw.py today — confirmed: it defines WRITE = 0x03 and never uses it, and has no 0x82/0x83 at all.
architecture.note: Sync write returns NO status packets, so a failed write is silent; only the next read verifies it. And sync_read replies come back in requested order, so if one servo is silent every later reply shifts onto the wrong joint — match the ID byte, which recv() currently discards.

architecture.job: CRC-16, byte stuffing, packet build and parse, error-byte decode.
architecture.interface: In: instruction + params. Out: bytes; and back.
architecture.size: dxl_raw.py, 288 lines, CRC verified byte-for-byte against three published ROBOTIS packets.
architecture.note: This is the one layer the entire field buys off the shelf (LeRobot, ALOHA and ROBOTIS all link DynamixelSDK). Writing it was a deliberate trade of ~3-4 days for visibility, not an oversight — and it is finished.

architecture.job: Open /dev/ttyACM0 raw at 1 Mbps with a bounded timeout, and guarantee exactly one process is on the bus.
architecture.interface: In: bytes. Out: bytes, or a timeout you can count.
architecture.size: ~55 lines written; ~30 more needed (select-based timeout, tcdrain, header resync, flock).
architecture.note: cc[VTIME]=1 is 100 ms granularity — 2.5 control periods per dropped reply. Fine for ping, fatal in a loop. And the termios backend has never executed, because the Dockerfile installs pyserial so open_port always takes the other branch.

architecture.layer: Servo firmware: profile generator + position PID
architecture.job: Generate a profile between goal positions and close the position loop at ~1 kHz inside each servo.
architecture.interface: In: ~10 register values. Out: shaft motion.
architecture.size: 0 lines. You choose about ten numbers per servo and otherwise cannot see inside it.
architecture.note: With P=1000 the loop saturates at 885/7.8125 = 113 pulses = 9.96 deg of error; beyond that it is bang-bang at full PWM. And I=0 means nothing nulls a constant gravity torque — the 6.48 mm droop is what a PD loop does under constant load, not a fault.

architecture.job: Hard stops, the 12 V / 5 V rails, cable routing, gravity, and the table.
architecture.size: 3-4 hours of measurement, ~20 lines of constants. Highest value per hour on the whole list.
architecture.note: The 6.48 mm droop was NOT measured at worst case: their pose loads joint2 at ~58% of the fully-horizontal gravity torque, so full extension is roughly 11 mm. Any table margin sized on 6.48 mm is undersized by ~75% exactly where a grasp ends.

architecture.job: Capture teleop episodes with image and proprioception timestamps aligned.
architecture.interface: In: camera + joint state. Out: a dataset the policy trains on.
architecture.size: 150-250 lines for a sync + recorder. Vendor contribution in the repo: 0 lines and one README link.
architecture.note: Nothing in the vendor tree subscribes to an image topic and joint states together. For an imitation-learning capstone this is a whole missing package, and choosing 'scripted policy, no recording' changes total scope more than anything at the servo layer.

ladder.verifyBy: Printed p50/p95/p99/max tick duration. Everything above the bus is unbuildable until this number is known and stable.

ladder.does: Moves the arm by hand to two known poses per joint, records ticks, solves sign and offset; finds the real hard stops and the gripper's true travel.

ladder.does: torque off -> EEPROM (modes, limits, current limit, shutdown) -> RAM (gains, profile, goal current) -> Goal := Present -> torque on.
ladder.verifyBy: Every register written is read back and diffed; the script refuses to proceed on any mismatch. Power-cycle and re-run: identical result.

ladder.title: Implement sync_write (0x83) and first commanded motion
ladder.does: One joint, small delta, from Goal := Present, at low profile speed.
ladder.verifyBy: Present Position converges to the commanded tick and stays there.

ladder.does: Set register 98 to 4-5 (80-100 ms), start a slow move, kill -9 the process, then unplug the USB mid-move.
ladder.verifyBy: Arm freezes in place rather than slamming or dropping; register 98 reads -1; writing 0 then the value restores it. Also settles whether a broadcast sync_write feeds the watchdog.

ladder.verifyBy: --hold holds the arm at its measured present pose through the full decode path without visible creep.

ladder.verifyBy: A full pick at real speed with p99 tick jitter under 3 ms and zero rejected chunks.

ladder.verifyBy: Re-measure droop at FULL horizontal extension, not the pose used for the 6.48 mm figure.

ladder.verifyBy: A written decision. This choice changes total scope more than anything below it.

synthesis.whereTheyAre: They are on rungs 4 and 5 of about nineteen: the packet codec is finished and CRC-verified, the kinematics and decoder are finished and validated to 3.24e-16 m, and s1_ping.py and s2_read.py are written but have never touched the robot. Everything they have built so far is read-only by construction — dxl_raw.py defines WRITE = 0x03 and never uses it, and has no sync_read or sync_write at all — so the entire second half of the driver, the half that moves the arm, has not started. The gating item is not code: it is the bench calibration at step 8, because every number in the existing 1,603 lines lives in the vendor's joint frame, applied by the C++ they cannot read.
scopeHonesty: Honest total for the replacement driver: about 1,200 lines of Python and roughly 2-3 weeks of one person's calendar time to reach 'trustworthy'. About 350 of those lines already exist. For comparison, DynamixelSDK's protocol-2 path alone is ~1,272 lines and dynamixel_hardware_interface on top of it is 4,710 lines of C++.

82% of what they already wrote survives untouched: of 1,603 lines in dummy_exec, exactly 107 touch ROS and 179 need dynamixel_sdk. All the maths moves as-is. They are not restarting; they are replacing the bottom third.

The remaining work is concentrated in four places: group transactions (~150 lines), the register init table with readback (~250-350), calibration (~40 lines plus half a day at the bench), and failsafe plus fault recovery (~250). Everything else is either done or small.

Legitimately skippable for a capstone: MoveIt (their analytic IK is strictly better on this arm — MoveIt's own config sets position_only_ik), URDF/TF/RViz, ros2_control entirely, FCL self-collision (a joint-space forbidden box is 20 lines and catches the case that matters), software interpolation (let the servo's profile generator smooth it), Fast Sync Read, and gravity-compensation torque control.

NOT skippable, and each one has already bitten someone: port exclusivity (3 lines of flock, and their teammate's PWM collision is exactly this bug), Goal := Present before Torque Enable = 1 (the most likely way to damage the arm during bring-up), readback-and-diff on every register write, polling Hardware Error Status (70), a per-joint software clamp, and measuring the loop period instead of assuming it.

The bench calibration is hours, not lines, and it gates everything above it. Until it is done, kinematics exact to 3.24e-16 m is exact arithmetic on the wrong numbers, and the error will look like a kinematic bug rather than a calibration one.

Writing the protocol codec yourself is unusual — LeRobot, ALOHA and ROBOTIS all link DynamixelSDK — but it cost about 3-4 days and it is the layer that made the tick mapping opaque. That trade is defensible. Writing your own init table and calibration is not unusual at all; it is what every lab does.

The rewrite does not automatically fix the original problem. Wrong gains present as droop, wrong profile semantics present as lag, a 100 ms timeout presents as jitter — all of which look like a bad policy. What fixes it is the readback-and-diff plus a per-tick log of commanded versus present position, maybe 60 lines total. Without those, they reproduce the same opacity in their own code.

Biggest scope decision, and it is not at the servo layer: whether the capstone records its own demonstrations. There is no recording or time-alignment code anywhere in the vendor tree — physical_ai_tools is a README link. A scripted or pretrained policy is the capstone-sized option; deciding late is what blows the budget.
surprises: The EEPROM/RAM boundary is address 64, and that single fact explains the 'registers silently resetting' mystery completely. Operating Mode, Drive Mode, Return Delay Time and the position limits persist; Position P/I/D Gain (80/82/84), Profile Acceleration (108) and Profile Velocity (112) do not. Profile Velocity 0 means INFINITE, not zero — so after a power cycle the first goal is a full-speed slam. [diy-scope, timing, safety]

Only two of six servos have any enforced position limit. joint1 (id 11) runs Operating Mode 4 (extended position) where the firmware ignores limits entirely, joints 4 and 5 are written 0..4095 which is the full range, and the gripper is Mode 5. Real bounds exist only on ids 12 (830..3129) and 13 (1024..3140). joint1 is the joint carrying the daisy-chain harness. [vendor-stack, safety, timing]

The 6.48 mm droop is arithmetic, not a fault. 6.48 mm at ~0.30 m reach = 14.1 pulses of error; with P=1000, KPP = 1000/128 = 7.8125 PWM/pulse, so 14.1 x 7.8125 = 110 PWM of 885 = 12.4% duty — a plausible gravity hold. With Position I Gain = 0 and no feedforward, a constant load gives a constant offset by construction. [timing]

The three joints that droop are the three that cannot be helped with current feedforward. XL430-W250 (ids 11/12/13) has no Current Limit (38), no Goal Current (102) and no Operating Mode 5. Only the XL330s can current-limit, so the gripper works and the shoulder does not. [our-position, diy-scope]

Return Delay Time (address 9) ships at 250, and the unit is 2 us — 500 us per servo, 3 ms across six, on every single read. Writing one byte to address 9 roughly quadruples the achievable loop rate, and it is EEPROM so it persists. Cheapest change on the entire list. [diy-scope, field-practice]

The bus is nowhere near the constraint. A sync_write of six goal positions is 44 bytes = 440 us; a sync_read is ~1.1 ms with RDT=0. A full cycle is ~1.5-1.9 ms, a 500-650 Hz ceiling, against a need of 25 Hz. USB CDC-ACM round-trip latency (1-3 ms, frame-quantized) is the real floor — and it is identical in C++, so a rewrite for speed would buy nothing. [timing, diy-scope, field-practice]

Jitter converted into the unit that matters: at 0.2 m/s end-effector speed, 1 ms = 0.20 mm and 10 ms = 2.00 mm. Their accepted 6.48 mm droop equals 32 ms of timing error. CPython on a non-RT Jetson gives p99 of 1-3 ms. Python is not the problem, and PREEMPT_RT is not the fix. [timing]

They were never getting velocity feedforward from JointTrajectoryController. The config declares command_interfaces: [position] only, so JTC was a pure open-loop spline sampler — the velocities in their messages shaped the spline and never reached the hardware. Dropping JTC costs them nothing. [timing]

Recovering a servo from Overload requires Reboot (0x08), and Reboot wipes the entire RAM area. So a stall during data collection silently reverts that joint to factory gains and zero profile mid-run, with no power cycle to blame. Recovery must replay the whole init block, not just re-enable torque. [safety, diy-scope]

Bus Watchdog (register 98, 20 ms units) freezes the arm holding position rather than dropping it, and it keeps working when the Jetson dies or the USB is yanked — which atexit and SIGTERM handlers do not. Corollary: a power-cutting e-stop is a worse safety device on this arm than the watchdog, because cutting power IS the drop. [safety, diy-scope]

The gripper's Shutdown = 21 deliberately CLEARS the Overload bit (default is 53) so it can stall against an object forever. Copy that value to an arm joint and you have disabled the only automatic guard against a joint cooking itself against the table; 'fix' it back to 53 on the gripper and it drops objects mid-pick. [vendor-stack, safety]

One researcher found that LeRobot upstream already ships a direct-serial driver for this exact robot — src/lerobot/robots/omx_follower/omx_follower.py, 231 lines, with ids 11-16 and the same model split — and that the tick mapping they could not read is a five-column text file, param/dxl_model/xl430_w250.model, containing 0.0015339807878856412 rad per tick, i.e. exactly 2*pi/4096 with a -pi offset. Worth 20 minutes to verify before writing anything. [field-practice]

Their own stack is already more sophisticated than the vendor's flagship imitation-learning tool: physical_ai_tools publishes a JointTrajectory with exactly one point and no time_from_start — a setpoint in a trajectory costume. [vendor-stack, field-practice]

A confirmed latent bug in their existing code: omx_kinematics.inverse wraps j5 into (-pi, pi], so commanding roll 179 deg then 180 deg makes joint5 jump 359 deg, which the velocity gate reads as 4,488 deg/s and rejects — the arm freezes with one warn line. Latent only because the scripted pick uses roll=0 throughout. [our-position]

Their s2_read.py treats the Alert bit (0x80) as a failed read, so the moment any servo has a hardware error the script prints '-' for every register and says 'every read failed' while the bus is perfectly healthy. Split err into alert = err & 0x80 and code = err & 0x7F. [safety]
disagreements: The biggest one, and it changes the design: what Profile Velocity = 50 means. Four views say Drive Mode = 4 sets bit 2 = TIME-BASED profile, so 50 is 50 milliseconds of move time and 25 is a 25 ms accel ramp — deliberately just longer than their 40 ms tick, so steps overlap and blend. One view (vendor-stack) read it as velocity-based and computed a ~1.20 rad/s speed cap, concluding the arm is silently rate-limited 4x below what the trajectory layer believes. These cannot both be true. Read Drive Mode bit 2 back from the servo and branch on it explicitly — and note the practical trap either way: copying '50' without copying '4' turns a 50 ms blend into a 5x speed cap that looks exactly like a policy that does not work.

Consequently the two views disagree on whether their MAX_JOINT_VEL = 180 deg/s guard is 2.6x too permissive (vendor-stack: firmware clamps at 1.2 rad/s first) or roughly half the real ceiling (safety: XL430 Velocity Limit register 44 gives 6.35 rad/s). Step 12's profile-lag experiment settles both with their own data.

Joint travel limits. One view cites ROBOTIS documentation for joint1 at -270..+360 deg and joint5 at +/-270 deg — both exceeding what Mode 3 can cover. Another derives joint2 = -107..+95 deg and joint3 = -90..+96 deg from the EEPROM tick limits. These describe different joints and may both be right, but nobody reconciled them, and the URDF's uniform +/-2pi contradicts all of it. Measure by hand.
Gripper model. ROBOTIS' hardware page lists the OMX-F gripper as XL330-M077-T (model 1190); both LeRobot and the ROBOTIS fork declare xl330-m288 (model 1200). s1_ping.py settles it in one run.

XL430 Position D Gain default: emanual.robotis.com says 4000, docs.robotis.com says 3600, and one view reported 4000 while another reported 3600. This is exactly the class of problem that started the rewrite; the only fix is reading the register back.

Their own tree disagrees with itself on the tick divisor: omx_kinematics.py documents /4095, s2_read.py and omx_probe.py use /4096. The spec is 4096. The numeric difference is negligible; the fact that no single file owns the conversion is not.

THIN EVIDENCE, needs a bench test before anything depends on it: whether a broadcast sync_write (ID 0xFE) resets each servo's Bus Watchdog. If it does not, the watchdog fires during normal operation. Not documented in the e-manual.

THIN EVIDENCE: whether Bus Watchdog behaves usefully in Position Control Mode at all. The only in-repo precedent (omy_f3m_current) is a current-control arm. Since the whole safety story rests on this, run the 20-minute kill -9 experiment first.
THIN EVIDENCE: whether a mid-profile Goal Position write regenerates from present velocity or from rest. This changes steady-state lag by roughly 5x and ROBOTIS does not document it.

SINGLE-SOURCE and unverified by the other five: the claim that LeRobot upstream ships omx_follower for this exact robot and that the tick constant is in a plain-text .model file. Load-bearing enough to check directly, cheap enough that checking costs 20 minutes.

Estimates of how much of the loop the USB round trip eats range from 1-2 ms to 6-24 ms depending on whether you sync or go per-servo. Nobody measured it on this Jetson. That is step 7 and it should precede every design decision above it.

layers.name: Failsafe / watchdog supervision
layers.whatItDoes: Decides what the arm does when the thing above it stops talking. Three independent mechanisms, and you want all three because each covers a different death: (a) Bus Watchdog, RAM address 98, 1 byte, unit 20 ms, range 1-127 (20 ms to 2540 ms) — firmware-side, so it still fires when your Python is SIGKILLed, the USB cable is yanked, or the Jetson hangs; (b) a SIGTERM/atexit handler that writes Goal Position(116) <- Present Position(132) and then decides about Torque Enable(64); (c) Startup Configuration(60) bit 0 left at 0 so a power cycle always brings the arm up limp. Confirmed behaviour of 98 on timeout: the servo stops, all goal registers become read-only and return a Data Range Error if written, and register 98 itself reads as -1. It is cleared by writing 0 to 98, then rewriting the desired value. Critically it does NOT clear Torque Enable — the arm freezes holding position rather than collapsing. For a 400 mm arm already showing 6.48 mm of gravity droop that is the correct failure mode, and it means 'fail safe' here is fail-stiff, not fail-limp: torque-off is only safe in a pose where falling is harmless. For a 25 Hz command stream (dt = 0.04 s) set 98 = 4 or 5 (80-100 ms). One thing I could NOT confirm in the e-manual: whether a broadcast Sync Write (ID 0xFE) resets each servo's watchdog, or only packets addressed to that specific ID. If it does not, the watchdog will fire during perfectly normal operation. Verify on the bench before trusting it.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself — no vendor stack ships a failsafe policy because the right answer is application-specific (hold vs. limp vs. retract), and ros2_control's own lifecycle only covers clean shutdown, not SIGKILL or a dead USB link

layers.name: Lifecycle and error-recovery state machine
layers.whatItDoes: Owns the torque sequence and the path back from a latched hardware fault. The torque sequence has one rule that is easy to get wrong and expensive: write Goal Position(116) <- Present Position(132) BEFORE writing Torque Enable(64) <- 1. Otherwise the servo torques on against whatever stale goal sits in RAM, and because Profile Velocity(112) defaults to 0 which means INFINITE velocity, it gets there as fast as the motor allows. The EEPROM rule: addresses 0-63 are writable only while Torque Enable(64) == 0; attempting otherwise returns error 7 (Access Error), which your ERRORS dict in dxl_raw.py already names correctly. Error detection: every status packet's ERR byte bit 7 is the Alert bit; when set, read Hardware Error Status(70) to find out which — bit 0 Input Voltage (0x01), bit 2 Overheating (0x04), bit 3 Motor Encoder (0x08), bit 4 Electrical Shock (0x10), bit 5 Overload (0x20). Which of those latch a shutdown is governed by the Shutdown register(63), an inclusive-OR mask, default 52 (0b00110100 = overheat + electrical shock + overload) on XL430 and 53 (0b00110101, same plus input voltage) on XL330 — note the XL430s do NOT have input-voltage shutdown armed by default. Recovery is the part people skip: the Clear instruction 0x10 with P1 = 0x02 ('ERCL') clears errors on Y series ONLY. On your X-series servos the only way out of a latched shutdown is Reboot (instruction 0x08) — which resets the entire RAM area back to defaults. So the recovery path must be: detect alert -> read 70 -> identify the servo -> Reboot 0x08 -> wait for re-enumeration -> replay the ENTIRE RAM config block for that one servo -> resync goal to present -> torque on. Not just 'set torque enable again'.

layers.name: Safety envelope: limits, rate, current
layers.whatItDoes: The clamp between decoded joint targets and Goal Position. Four separate jobs. (1) Position limits: Max Position Limit(48) and Min Position Limit(52), 4 bytes each, EEPROM, unit 1 pulse. These are firmware-enforced and are the only limit source that cannot lie to you — which is why s2_read.py reading them is the right instinct. BUT they are only enforced in Operating Mode 3. This matters enormously for your arm: ROBOTIS documents joint 1 as -270 deg to +360 deg (a 630 deg span) and joint 5 as +/-270 deg (540 deg), both of which exceed the 360 deg that mode 3 covers. Those two joints must run in Extended Position Control (mode 4), where the Goal Position range becomes +/-1,048,575 pulses and 48/52 stop clamping. For joints 1 and 5, software is the only limit. (2) Rate limiting on the delta between consecutive Goal Positions — a policy that emits a bad chunk will otherwise command a full-scale step. (3) Current limiting: Current Limit(38), 2 bytes, EEPROM, unit 1 mA, default and max 1750 mA, and Goal Current(102), 2 bytes, RAM, unit 1 mA. In Operating Mode 5 (Current-based Position Control) 102 caps what the position loop is allowed to draw — this is the correct way to run the gripper on a deformable object. Hard constraint: XL430-W250 has NEITHER register. No Current Limit at 38, no Goal Current at 102, and no mode 5. Only ids 14, 15, 16 can current-limit. Your gripper is id 16 (XL330-M288), so gripper force control works; joints 1-3 have only PWM Limit(36), 2 bytes, unit 0.113%, max 885 = 100%. (4) Following-error watch: Moving Status(123) bit 3 set means the servo is not tracking its trajectory — a cheap collision hint.

layers.name: Units and calibration: ticks <-> radians
layers.whatItDoes: One formula, theta = (tick - tick_zero) * (2*pi/4096) * dir, and every term in it has to be measured rather than assumed. Resolution is 4096 pulses/rev on BOTH models, so 1 tick = 0.087890625 deg = 1.53398e-3 rad, and the gear ratios (258.5:1 on XL430, 288:1 on XL330) do not enter — the encoder count is at the output shaft. The reasons you cannot assume tick_zero = 2048: (a) Homing Offset, address 20, 4 bytes, EEPROM, unit 1 pulse, range +/-1,044,479, applies as Present Position(132) = Actual Position + Homing Offset(20) — it is persistent and the vendor may already have set it nonzero; (b) Drive Mode(10) bit 0 flips the sign of Goal AND Present Position but explicitly does NOT flip Homing Offset, so sign and offset do not compose the way you would expect; (c) in mode 3 the e-manual says Homing Offset values outside -1024..+1024 are silently ignored, so a value you write may not take effect; (d) your FK/IK zero is a robot convention that lived in the external C++ package you cannot read — there is no reason for it to coincide with a servo convention. The only honest procedure is two-pose calibration with torque off: put the arm in known pose A (hard stops, a printed jig, or visually straight-up), Sync Read 132 on all six, record; repeat at known pose B. Two poses give you offset AND sign AND a check on the 2*pi/4096 scale, per joint. Also decide where the offset LIVES: host-side in your repo (diffable, survives a factory reset, my recommendation) or servo-side in register 20 (invisible, and silently erased by Factory Reset 0x06). Other units you will need: Profile Velocity 0.229 rev/min per unit = 0.023981 rad/s per unit (so 1 rad/s = 41.70 units); Profile Acceleration 214.577 rev/min^2 per unit = 0.374524 rad/s^2 per unit (1 rad/s^2 = 2.670 units); Present Load on XL430 address 126 is 0.1% of max torque in -1000..1000, but the SAME address 126 on XL330 is Present Current in mA. Different physical quantity, same address.

layers.name: Servo configuration model (the power-on register block)
layers.whatItDoes: The named, version-controlled answer to 'what settings is this arm actually running'. This is the direct fix for the problem that drove the rewrite. The exact block, in order, per servo. VERIFY FIRST, no writes: Model Number(0, 2 bytes) must read 1060 on ids 11/12/13 and 1200 on 14/15/16; Firmware Version(6, 1 byte) — you need v42+ for time-based profile, v45+ (X430) / v46+ (X330) for Startup Configuration RAM restore and Control Table Backup; Baud Rate(8) == 3 for 1 Mbps; Hardware Error Status(70) == 0 before you do anything else. THEN Torque Enable(64) <- 0, and only now the EEPROM writes, each guarded by a readback so you do not burn write cycles: Return Delay Time(9) <- 0 (default is 250, and the unit is 2 us, so the default costs 500 us per servo per reply); Drive Mode(10) — bit 0 direction, bit 2 profile type (0 = velocity-based, 1 = time-based), bit 3 leave at 0 so torque-on stays explicit; Operating Mode(11) — 3 for joints 2/3/4, 4 for joints 1 and 5 because their travel exceeds 360 deg, 5 for the gripper id 16; Homing Offset(20); Temperature Limit(31, default 72 on XL430 / 70 on XL330); PWM Limit(36); Current Limit(38) on ids 14/15/16 ONLY — this register does not exist on XL430 and writing it will error; Velocity Limit(44, defaults 265 on XL430 = 6.35 rad/s, 445 on XL330 = 10.67 rad/s); Max/Min Position Limit(48/52); Startup Configuration(60) bit 1 <- 1 for RAM restore, bit 0 <- 0; Shutdown(63). THEN the RAM block, still with torque off: Velocity I/P Gain(76/78); Position D Gain(80) — default 4000 on XL430 but 0 on XL330, so ids 14/15/16 ship with no derivative term at all; Position I Gain(82) — 0 on all six, and KPI = table/65536 is the register aimed straight at your 6.48 mm droop; Position P Gain(84) — 640 on XL430, 400 on XL330, KPP = table/128; Feedforward 1st/2nd Gain(90/88), both 0, KFF = table/4; Bus Watchdog(98); Goal Current(102) on the gripper; Profile Acceleration(108); Profile Velocity(112) — MUST be nonzero, because 0 means infinite; optionally the Indirect Address block(168-222, RAM, resets on power cycle) to gather non-contiguous telemetry into one Sync-Readable run; Goal Position(116) <- Present Position(132); and LAST, Torque Enable(64) <- 1. On RAM persistence: Startup Configuration(60) bit 1 restores RAM at boot, but it requires firmware v45+/v46+ AND a prior Control Table Backup (instruction 0x20, P1 = 0x01, P2-P5 = 0x43 0x54 0x52 0x4C) issued with torque off. That combination is the documented answer to 'RAM registers silently resetting on power cycle'. Even so, write the block explicitly every boot — it costs 3 ms and it means the config in your git repo is the config on the wire.

layers.name: Group transaction scheduler (Sync Write / Sync Read)
layers.whatItDoes: Turns six servos into one bus transaction. Sync Write (0x83): ID field is 0xFE broadcast, params are ADDR_L, ADDR_H, LEN_L, LEN_H then a repeating [ID, data...] run. For 6 servos x 4-byte Goal Position that is 4 + 6*5 = 34 param bytes, total packet 4+1+2+1+34+2 = 44 bytes = 440 us at 1 Mbps, and NO status packets come back at all. Sync Read (0x82): same 4-byte header then a bare list of IDs; 6 IDs gives a 20-byte request, and each servo replies with its own separate status packet of 11 + N bytes. Reading 4 bytes each: 6 x 15 bytes = 900 us, so 1.10 ms per full state read with Return Delay Time at 0. With the factory default RDT of 250 (500 us each) the same read costs 4.10 ms — the single byte at address 9 is roughly 4x on your loop rate. Reading the contiguous 126..135 run (Present Load/Current, Present Velocity, Present Position, 10 bytes) costs 1.46 ms. So a full cycle of one Sync Write plus one 10-byte Sync Read is about 1.9 ms of wire time: a ~525 Hz ceiling from the serial link alone. Your actual need is 25 Hz (dt = 0.04 s, H = 16 = a 640 ms horizon), so the bus has roughly 20x headroom and is NOT your bottleneck — USB CDC-ACM round-trip latency on /dev/ttyACM0 is, and it will realistically put you at 100-300 Hz. That is still 4-12x your chunk rate, which is what makes receding-horizon streaming comfortable. Why Sync matters is not really the 440 us: six individual writes cost 1620 us of wire but SIX separate USB round trips, and each of those is ~0.5-2 ms of scheduling latency regardless of baud. Sync Write collapses six USB transactions into one. Bulk Read (0x92) / Bulk Write (0x93) take per-device [ID, ADDR_L, ADDR_H, LEN_L, LEN_H] tuples and are what you need when the XL430s and XL330s must be addressed at different registers in the same cycle — e.g. Present Load on 11/12/13 versus Present Current on 14/15/16, same address 126 but different meaning. Fast Sync Read (0x8A) folds all six replies into ONE status packet with per-device CRCs and no byte stuffing; it needs FW v45+ on X430 and v46+ on X330, and it is the single biggest latency win available if your firmware supports it. One demux rule that is easy to miss: replies come back in the order the IDs were listed, so if one servo is silent every subsequent reply shifts onto the wrong joint. You must match the ID byte in each status packet, not rely on position.

layers.name: Protocol 2.0 packet codec
layers.whatItDoes: Header FF FF FD 00, reserved byte, ID, 2-byte little-endian length counting INST + PARAMS + CRC, instruction, params, CRC-16 (poly 0x8005, init 0x0000, MSB first, no final xor) over everything preceding. Byte stuffing inserts an extra 0xFD after any literal FF FF FD in the payload, the length field counts stuffed bytes, and the CRC is computed over the stuffed body. Status packets carry INST = 0x55 and one extra ERR byte: bits 0-6 are the error number (1 result fail, 2 instruction, 3 CRC, 4 data range, 5 data length, 6 data limit, 7 access/EEPROM-while-torqued) and bit 7 is the Alert flag meaning 'also check Hardware Error Status(70)'. You are done here. dxl_raw.py implements all of it and validates the CRC byte-for-byte against three published ROBOTIS example packets, which is the correct way to prove a codec without hardware.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: off-the-shelf in dynamixel_sdk, but it is the most self-contained and most testable layer in the stack and you have already written it. Keep it

layers.name: Byte transport: half duplex, timeouts, retries, recovery
layers.whatItDoes: One wire, one talker, strict write-then-read. What is still missing from your _RawSerial. (1) Timeout granularity: you set VMIN = 0 and VTIME = 1, which is a 100 ms tick, and Bus() defaults to timeout = 0.1 s. Expected reply time for a 15-byte status packet with Return Delay Time at 0 is about 200 us — you are budgeting 500x that, so one dropped reply costs 100 ms, i.e. 2.5 whole control cycles at 25 Hz. For the control loop you want VTIME = 0 plus select()/poll() with a ~3 ms budget; keep the generous timeout only for ping and config. (2) Half-duplex turnaround: send() calls reset_input_buffer() BEFORE writing but never tcdrain()s after. os.write returns once the kernel has buffered the bytes, not once they are on the wire, so if your USB-TTL converter echoes (many do) you can read back the tail of your own packet. Right order is flush input, write, tcdrain, read. Test it with s1_ping before trusting it. (3) Resync: recv() gives up if head[:4] != HEADER. Better to scan forward for FF FF FD 00 — the e-manual notes that an inter-byte gap over 1.5 ms triggers the servo's own resynchronization, so partial-packet garbage is a normal condition, not a fatal one. (4) Reply identity: recv() returns (err, params, raw) and discards raw[4], the ID. That is fine for one-to-one reads and wrong for Sync Read, where you must attribute each of six replies to the right joint. (5) Retry policy: reads are idempotent, retry up to 2x within the cycle. All DYNAMIXEL writes are absolute rather than incremental, so retrying a Goal Position write is also safe — but never carry a retry into the next control cycle; drop the cycle instead. Escalate on consecutive failures: 1 log, 3 stop issuing new goals, 5 hold and abort. (6) Port exclusivity: take an flock() on the device, or an O_EXCL lockfile. Your run.sh already greps for a running ros2_control_node, which is a good instinct, but a grep is advisory and racy — a flock is 10 lines and permanently ends the class of bug where a teammate's PWM script collides with yours on the same /dev/ttyACM0. (7) Note that /dev/ttyACM0 is CDC-ACM, not FTDI, so the usual latency_timer fix (writing 1 to /sys/bus/usb-serial/.../latency_timer) does not apply here — measure your actual round-trip instead of assuming it.

The advisory ros2_control check is in dxl_basics/run.sh. The 1.5 ms inter-byte resynchronization threshold is documented at emanual.robotis.com/docs/en/dxl/protocol2/.

With a 0.1 s timeout you stall for four control cycles, the receding horizon underruns, and the arm executes stale goals. Worse, with no ID checking on Sync Read replies, one silent servo silently reassigns every subsequent reply to the wrong joint and your state estimate is confidently wrong rather than obviously broken.

keyFindings: Return Delay Time (address 9, 1 byte, unit 2 us) ships at 250 = 500 us per servo per reply. Across six servos that is 3.0 ms added to every Sync Read. A 4-byte Sync Read costs 1.10 ms with RDT=0 and 4.10 ms with the default — writing one byte to address 9 roughly quadruples your achievable loop rate. It is the cheapest change on this entire list.

Timing at 1 Mbps (10 us/byte, 8N1): Sync Write of six 4-byte Goal Positions = 44 bytes = 440 us, no replies. Sync Read of 4 bytes from six = 20-byte request + 6 x 15-byte replies = 1.10 ms. Reading the contiguous 126..135 block (load/current, velocity, position) = 1.46 ms. Full cycle ~1.9 ms => ~525 Hz wire ceiling. Your need is 25 Hz (dt=0.04, H=16 = 640 ms horizon), so the bus has ~20x headroom. USB CDC-ACM round-trip latency, not the serial link, will be your limit — expect 100-300 Hz in practice.

The real argument for Sync Write is not wire time. Six individual writes cost 1620 us of wire but six separate USB round trips at ~0.5-2 ms of scheduling latency each. Sync Write collapses that to one transaction, which also means all six joints receive their goal in the same packet instead of milliseconds apart.

XL430-W250 has NO Current Limit (38) and NO Goal Current (102), and does not support Operating Mode 5 (Current-based Position Control). Only PWM Limit (36, unit 0.113%, max 885) exists. So ids 11/12/13 cannot be current-limited at all; only the three XL330s (14/15/16) can. Your gripper is id 16, an XL330-M288, so Goal Current gripping does work — for the gripper only.

Position D Gain (80) defaults to 4000 on XL430 but 0 on XL330. Joints 4, 5 and the gripper ship with no derivative term. Position I Gain (82) defaults to 0 on all six — and KPI = table_value / 65536 is the register most directly aimed at your measured 6.48 mm of gravity droop, since integral action is what removes a constant load-induced steady-state error.

ROBOTIS documents joint 1 as -270 deg to +360 deg (630 deg of travel) and joint 5 as +/-270 deg (540 deg). Both exceed the 360 deg that Operating Mode 3 covers, so those two joints need Extended Position Control (mode 4) — where Goal Position range becomes +/-1,048,575 pulses and Max/Min Position Limit (48/52) are no longer firmware-enforced. For joints 1 and 5, your software is the only limit that exists.

Profile Velocity (112) defaults to 0, and 0 means INFINITE velocity, not zero. Profile Acceleration (108) default 0 likewise means infinite. Both are RAM, so both reset on every power cycle. If you torque on before writing them, the first goal position is executed at maximum motor speed.

Drive Mode (10) bit 2 = 1 selects time-based profile (firmware v42+), which redefines Profile Velocity (112) as total move time in ms and Profile Acceleration (108) as acceleration ramp time in ms, constrained to accel <= 50% of the total. Setting 112 = 40 and 108 = 16 makes every Sync Write a 40 ms time-parameterized move that lands exactly when the next chunk step arrives. That is an exact match to your dt = 0.04 s, and it hands the interpolation to the servo's own profile generator instead of your Python.

Unit conversions, confirmed: 1 tick = 2*pi/4096 = 1.53398e-3 rad = 0.087890625 deg, on both models (encoder is at the output shaft, so the 258.5:1 and 288:1 gear ratios do not enter). Profile Velocity unit 0.229 rev/min = 0.023981 rad/s, so 1 rad/s = 41.70 units. Profile Acceleration unit 214.577 rev/min^2 = 0.374524 rad/s^2, so 1 rad/s^2 = 2.670 units. Gain scaling: KPP = table/128, KPI = table/65536, KPD = table/16, KFF = table/4.

Address 126 is Present Load on XL430 (unit 0.1% of max torque, range -1000..1000) and Present Current on XL330 (unit 1 mA). Same address, different physical quantity, on the same bus. This is exactly what Bulk Read (0x92) exists for. s2_read.py already notes this in a comment but the code still labels all six 'Present Load'.

On X-series servos the Clear instruction (0x10) with P1 = 0x02 clears errors on Y series ONLY. Your only route out of a latched Shutdown is Reboot (0x08) — which wipes the entire RAM area back to defaults. So fault recovery is not 're-enable torque'; it is reboot, wait for re-enumeration, replay the whole RAM config block for that servo, resync goal to present, then torque on.

Startup Configuration (address 60) bit 1 = RAM Restore is the documented answer to 'RAM registers silently reset on power cycle'. It requires firmware v45+ (X430) / v46+ (X330) AND a prior Control Table Backup (instruction 0x20, P1 = 0x01, P2-P5 = 0x43 0x54 0x52 0x4C) issued with Torque Enable = 0. Bit 0 (Startup Torque On) should stay 0 so a power cycle always brings the arm up limp.

Bus Watchdog (98, unit 20 ms, range 1-127 => 20-2540 ms) stops motion and makes all goal registers read-only on timeout, with register 98 reading -1; you clear it by writing 0 then rewriting the value. Critically it does NOT clear Torque Enable — the arm freezes holding position rather than collapsing. For a 400 mm arm with 6.48 mm of droop that is the right failure mode, and it means 'safe' here is fail-stiff, not fail-limp.

Shutdown register (63) defaults differ across your own arm: 52 on XL430 (overheat + electrical shock + overload) and 53 on XL330 (same plus input voltage, bit 0). The three XL430s carrying most of the arm's mass do not have input-voltage shutdown armed out of the box.

Total honest size for the replacement driver: roughly 1200 lines of Python and about 2 weeks of one person's calendar time to reach 'trustworthy', of which ~350 lines already exist (the Protocol 2.0 codec is done and CRC-verified; the termios transport is ~60 of its ~150 lines). tripwires: _RawSerial sets VTIME = 1, which is a 100 ms granularity, and Bus() defaults to timeout = 0.1 s — about 500x the ~200 us a 15-byte reply actually takes. One dropped reply stalls you for 2.5 control cycles at 25 Hz. Switch the control path to VTIME = 0 plus select() with a ~3 ms budget; keep the generous timeout for ping and config only.

Bus.send() calls reset_input_buffer() before writing but never tcdrain()s after. os.write returns when the kernel buffers the bytes, not when they are on the wire, so on an echoing USB-TTL converter you can read back the tail of your own 440 us Sync Write. Correct order is flush input, write, tcdrain, read. Confirm empirically with s1_ping before building on it.

Bus.recv() discards raw[4], the reply's ID byte. Sync Read returns six separate status packets in the order the IDs were requested — if one servo is silent, every subsequent reply shifts onto the wrong joint and your state estimate is confidently wrong rather than obviously broken. You must match the ID, not the position.

Writing Current Limit (38) or Goal Current (102) to ids 11/12/13 will fail: those registers do not exist on XL430-W250. If your config block is a single flat table applied to all six servos, it will error on half the arm.

Torque Enable (64) <- 1 before Goal Position (116) <- Present Position (132) makes the servo drive to whatever stale goal is in RAM, at infinite speed because Profile Velocity (112) defaults to 0. This single ordering mistake is the most likely way to damage the arm during bring-up.

Whether a broadcast Sync Write (ID 0xFE) resets each servo's Bus Watchdog, or whether only directly-addressed packets do, is NOT clearly documented in the e-manual and I could not confirm it. If broadcasts do not feed the watchdog, it will fire in the middle of normal operation. Test this deliberately before relying on the watchdog as your failsafe.

Drive Mode (10) and Operating Mode (11) are EEPROM: torque must be 0 to write them, and EEPROM has finite write endurance. Always read back first and write only on a mismatch — do not blind-write the EEPROM block every boot.

Take an flock() on /dev/ttyACM0. run.sh greps for a running ros2_control_node, which is the right instinct, but a grep is advisory and racy, and it does not see a teammate's PWM script at all. Ten lines of flock permanently closes the exact failure that already cost you once.

Rebooting a servo to clear an Overload wipes its RAM: gains, profile, watchdog, goal, indirect addresses, all back to defaults. The recovery path must replay the entire RAM config block for that servo, not just set Torque Enable again.

s2_read.py hardcodes CENTER = 2048 and its own comment correctly calls this 'a hypothesis, not a fact'. Homing Offset (20) is EEPROM and may already be nonzero from the vendor's calibration, and Drive Mode bit 0 inverts Goal and Present Position but explicitly not Homing Offset — so sign and offset do not compose the way you would expect. Measure both, at two known poses, before trusting any angle.

Keep the tick-zero offsets host-side in your repo rather than in Homing Offset (20). A number in git is diffable and survives a Factory Reset (0x06); a number in EEPROM is invisible and is silently erased by one. The tradeoff: if Homing Offset stays 0, your software position limits have to be expressed in raw ticks too, in the same frame the firmware uses.

Fast Sync Read (0x8A) collapses all six replies into one status packet and is the single biggest latency win available — but it needs FW v45+ on the X430s and v46+ on the X330s. Read Firmware Version (address 6) on all six during bring-up and record it; if the arm is on older firmware, half the good options on this list (time-based profile needs v42+, RAM restore needs v45+/v46+) are simply not there.

keyFindings: There is ZERO DYNAMIXEL protocol code in the vendor repo. A grep across every .py/.cpp/.hpp/.xacro/.yaml for termios|PortHandler|PacketHandler|GroupSyncWrite|GroupSyncRead|crc16|protocol_version returns only port-name strings and keyboard raw-mode termios in the four teleop scripts. Everything that forms a packet lives in DynamixelSDK + dynamixel_hardware_interface, which are cloned into the container by docker/Dockerfile:58-60 and are not present anywhere on the host disk. The repo's entire hardware contribution is 12 XML parameter lines per robot (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:18-30).

ROBOTIS's OMX-AI-follower-specific contribution is 1,577 lines across 14 files, and the live runtime path is ~823 of those: omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py 205, config 51 (32+19), omx_f.ros2_control.xacro 179, URDF xacro 338, gazebo xacro 50. The whole repo is 23,299 lines of code+config across 11 packages, of which open_manipulator_gui is the single largest at 11,283 lines (6,582 of them Qt .ui XML) and is entirely irrelevant to this project.

The joint limits disagree FOUR ways, not three. (1) URDF: every one of the 7 joints gets lower=-6.283185307179586, upper=+6.283185307179586, velocity=4.8, effort=1000 -- identical, i.e. no real limit (omx_f_arm.urdf.xacro:37,72,107,142,177,212,247). (2) MoveIt joint_limits.yaml sets NO position limits at all, only max_velocity 5.0 and max_acceleration 5.0 -- and 5.0 > the URDF's 4.8, so MoveIt raises the velocity limit. (3) ros2_control tick limits exist on only 4 of 6 servos: dxl12 830-3129, dxl13 1024-3140, dxl14 and dxl15 0-4095 (i.e. no limit). At 2*pi/4096 = 0.00153398 rad/tick about a 2048 center, that is joint2 = -107.1 deg to +95.0 deg and joint3 = -90.0 deg to +96.0 deg. The URDF therefore overstates joint2's usable travel by about 3.4x on the negative side and 3.8x on the positive side. (4) The servo motion profile is a fourth, invisible limit -- see next finding.

Profile Velocity 50 and Profile Acceleration 25 are set on all six servos (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:87-88 and repeats). At the X-series units of 0.229 rev/min and 214.577 rev/min^2 that is approximately 1.20 rad/s and 9.36 rad/s^2 at the output. The URDF advertises 4.8 rad/s and MoveIt asks for 5.0 rad/s. So the trajectory layer believes it can move about 4x faster than the firmware will allow. Any chunk step that implies more than ~1.2 rad/s is silently rate-limited by the servo, not rejected -- the arm just lags.

joint1 (id 11) runs Operating Mode 4 = Extended Position (multi-turn) and is the ONLY joint with no Min Position Limit and no Max Position Limit in the xacro (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:75-89). In extended position mode the firmware position limits are ignored by design. Combined with the URDF's +/-2pi and MoveIt's absent position limits, there is no software OR firmware bound on the yaw joint that carries the wiring harness. A single IK branch flip can wind it multiple turns.

The gripper (id 16) is Operating Mode 5 = current-based position control with Current Limit 600, Goal Current 600 and Shutdown 21 (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:158-175). Shutdown 21 = 0b010101 = bits 0, 2, 4. On the X-series shutdown mask, that turns ON input-voltage and overheating protection but leaves bit 5 (Overload Error) CLEAR, where the factory default 52 has it set. That is deliberate: the gripper is allowed to stall against an object indefinitely without tripping into torque-off.

The follower has no gravity compensation at any layer, and the droop is structural. Position I Gain = 0 on all six servos and no feedforward gain registers are set (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:85,102,118,136,153,168 -- P=1000, I=0, D=1000 on every one). A PD loop with no integral term and no gravity feedforward has a nonzero steady-state error under a constant load by construction. The measured 6.48 mm is the expected behavior of this configuration, not a fault.

The only gravity-compensation code ROBOTIS ships (832 lines) is for the LEADER arm, and as checked in it cannot activate on the OMX leader at all. omx_l_leader_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:27-28 asks the controller for `effort` command interfaces, but omx_l.ros2_control.xacro:36,42,48,54,60 has every single `<command_interface name="effort"/>` commented out, and :75,87,99,111,123 likewise comment out `Goal Current`. on_activate calls get_ordered_interfaces for 'effort' and would find zero, returning CallbackReturn::ERROR.

Which registers survive a power cycle is now precisely nameable, and it matches the user's complaint exactly. Of the values the xacro writes: Operating Mode, Drive Mode, Return Delay Time, Min/Max Position Limit, Current Limit and Shutdown are EEPROM (addresses 0-63) and persist. Position P/I/D Gain, Profile Velocity, Profile Acceleration and Goal Current are RAM (address 64+) and revert to factory defaults on every power cycle. That is why the vendor stack rewrites them on every bringup -- and why the team's own init sequence must do the same or the arm behaves differently after a power blip.

Four different serial-port defaults exist for the same two arms across seven files: omx_f.launch.py:61 and omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py:71 say /dev/ttyACM0; omx_f.urdf.xacro:9 and omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:3 say /dev/ttyACM1; omx_l_leader_ai.launch.py:60 says /dev/ttyACM2; omx_l.urdf.xacro:7 says /dev/ttyACM1; omx_l.ros2_control.xacro:3 says /dev/ttyACM0. The launch argument wins at runtime, but anyone who runs xacro by hand gets ACM1.

The OMX follower is the neglected sibling of the OMY. omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:4 sets update_rate 100 Hz and nothing else; omy_f3m_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml:4-6 sets update_rate 400, thread_priority 40 and cpu_affinity [1,2,3]. Same file, same purpose, 4x the rate and real-time scheduling for the OMY only. One control cycle on the OMX is 10 ms against a chunk dt of 40 ms.

The AI path and the MoveIt path are mutually incompatible as configured. omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml declares only joint_state_broadcaster and arm_controller, with gripper_joint_1 folded in as the 6th joint of the arm trajectory -- grep for gripper_controller in that file and in the launch returns 0. But open_manipulator_moveit_config/config/omx_f/moveit_controllers.yaml:19-23 expects a gripper_controller with a GripperCommand action, and omx_f.launch.py:152-159 (the non-AI launch) does spawn one. Running MoveIt against the AI bringup gives you a controller manager that cannot fulfill the gripper half of any plan.

The teleop data path the team's chunk executor is impersonating publishes a single trajectory point with time_from_start = 0 at the full controller rate. joint_trajectory_command_broadcaster.cpp:312-336 does points.resize(1) then sets time_from_start to Duration(0,0) with the comment 'immediate'. The Cartesian MoveL solver the OMX playground demo depends on is not in this repo. omx_trajectory_controller_node.py:25 imports MoveL from robotis_interfaces (a message package, cloned separately) and :95 publishes it to /omx_movel_controller/movel. grep for 'movel' across the whole tree finds only that one file -- nine references, all publishing. The self-collision node is hardcoded for the OMY-F3M and will not run on the OMX. self_collision_node.cpp:33-47 is a C++ initializer list of 13 link pairs referencing `end_effector_flange_link`, which occurs 4 times in omy_f3m.urdf and 0 times in omx_f.urdf, and self_collision.launch.py:26-31 hardcodes omy_f3m.urdf.xacro with tip_link 'rh_p12_rn_base'. The udev rule shipped for this robot cannot match it. open-manipulator-cdc.rules:1 is `KERNEL=="ttyACM*", DRIVERS=="ftdi_sio", MODE="0666", ATTR{device/latency_timer}="1"`. An ftdi_sio device enumerates as ttyUSB, not ttyACM; a ttyACM device binds cdc_acm. Line 1 matches nothing. The file is named 'cdc.rules' but neither line applies to a CDC device.

docker/workspace is gitignored (docker/.gitignore:1 is `workspace/`), so the team's own 1,067 lines of chunk executor, kinematics and dummy policy currently live inside a vendor checkout, untracked, and mounted into the container by docker-compose.yml:26. `git status --short` on the vendor repo shows only docker-compose.override.yml -- their entire working codebase is invisible to git.

MoveIt's own config concedes the 5-DOF problem the team already solved analytically: kinematics.yaml:5 sets `position_only_ik: True` with a 5 ms solver timeout. ROBOTIS's answer to 'this arm cannot reach arbitrary orientations' is to stop asking for orientation. The team's 5-DOF projection that forces EE yaw to atan2(y, x - BASE_X) is strictly more informative than what ships.

The gravity compensation controller allocates its KDL solver and four JntArrays inside update(), i.e. on every control cycle (gravity_compensation_controller.cpp:86-90). At the leader's 100 Hz that is 500 heap allocations per second inside what is supposed to be a real-time loop. Whatever else it is, it is not an example to copy.
tripwires: The container can grab /dev/ttyACM0 out from under your bare-metal scripts, and it is configured to come back. docker-compose.yml:9 is `restart: always`, :29 is privileged, :22 mounts all of /dev. docker/s6-services/open_manipulator_bringup/run:18-19 auto-launches omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py whenever /run/robot_type contains 'omx'. Before running s1_ping.py, check `cat /run/robot_type`, check the s6 service state, and confirm with `fuser /dev/ttyACM0` -- `docker stop` alone will not hold if the restart policy or s6 brings it back.

Half-duplex contention does not produce a clean error. Two masters on one bus produce CRC mismatches, phantom timeouts, and status packets attributed to the wrong servo. Your dxl_raw.py will report 'no response from id 14' when the real cause is that ros2_control answered id 14's slot. Build a single-owner check into run.sh before you debug a protocol bug that is not there.

Position P/I/D Gain, Profile Velocity, Profile Acceleration and Goal Current are RAM registers and revert on every power cycle -- that is the silent reset the user hit. Your init sequence must rewrite P=1000, I=0, D=1000, Profile Velocity 50, Profile Acceleration 25 and (for id 16) Goal Current 600 every single bringup. Operating Mode, Drive Mode, the tick limits, Current Limit and Shutdown are EEPROM and persist, but writing EEPROM requires torque off first -- which is exactly why the vendor sets disable_torque_at_init=true.

Do not 'fix' the gripper's Shutdown register back to the default 52. Shutdown 21 deliberately leaves the Overload bit clear so id 16 can stall against a grasped object. Restore 52 and the gripper will trip into torque-off mid-pick, drop the object, and look like a grasp-policy failure.

Do not trust the URDF as a safety limit. Every joint reads +/-2pi, MoveIt adds no position limit at all, and joint1 is in Extended Position mode with no firmware limit either. The only real bounds are the EEPROM tick limits on ids 12 and 13. Put your own per-joint clamp in the decoder, derived from the tick limits (joint2 about -107 to +95 deg, joint3 about -90 to +96 deg), before you run a policy whose outputs you have not seen.

Your 6.48 mm droop will not go away by tuning the trajectory. With I=0 and no feedforward, a PD loop under constant gravity torque has a constant offset by construction. The three real options are: raise Position I Gain (a RAM register -- it resets, so it must be in your init), switch the loaded joints to current-based position control with a feedforward torque, or add a constant per-joint offset measured empirically. The vendor stack offers none of these on the follower.

Profile Velocity 50 caps every joint at about 1.20 rad/s. Your chunks are dt = 0.04 s, so any step asking for more than ~0.048 rad (2.7 deg) of travel on a single joint gets rate-limited by firmware, and the arm falls behind the trajectory with no error anywhere. Their own MAX_JOINT_VEL guard is set to 180 deg/s = 3.14 rad/s, which is 2.6x above what the servo will actually deliver -- that guard will never fire before the firmware clamps.

The 100 Hz controller_manager rate on the OMX is not real-time scheduled -- no thread_priority, no cpu_affinity, unlike the OMY's 400 Hz + priority 40 + pinned cores. On a Jetson Orin also running a policy, image capture and Docker, expect jitter on the write cycle. If you write your own loop, you inherit this problem rather than escaping it; budget for measuring actual cycle times, not assuming them.

`is_async="true"` on the follower's ros2_control system (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro:4) means hardware read/write runs on its own thread, decoupled from the 100 Hz update. So the joint positions a controller sees are not synchronous with the bus transaction that produced them. If you reproduce this architecture, you inherit an unspecified age on every state reading; if you write a synchronous loop instead, your latency story becomes simpler and measurable -- which is an argument in favor of the rewrite.

robotis_interfaces and dynamixel_hardware_interface are excluded from rosdep everywhere (ros-ci.yml:60,62 --skip-keys, Dockerfile:69 same). If you ever rebuild the workspace outside the prebuilt image, those two will not resolve from apt and must come from open_manipulator_ci.repos via vcs. A colcon build that 'mysteriously' loses the hardware plugin is this.

Move your own code out of docker/workspace/. It is gitignored by the vendor's docker/.gitignore, so 1,067 lines of your chunk executor, kinematics and policy are sitting untracked inside someone else's repo. One `git clean -xfd` in that directory and it is gone. Give it its own repo and bind-mount it.

Zenoh, not DDS. RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp with ROS_DOMAIN_ID=30. A node started outside the container, or inside it without those env vars, will see an empty graph and report nothing wrong. Check `ros2 topic list` returns the arm's topics before concluding your publisher is broken.

Budget the MoveIt decision now, not later. The AI bringup declares no gripper_controller while moveit_controllers.yaml demands one, so MoveIt and follower_ai cannot both be right. Given they already have validated analytic IK to 3.4e-16 m and MoveIt's own config admits position-only IK on this arm, MoveIt is the easiest ~1,151 lines of dependency to drop -- but drop it deliberately, because the SRDF's disable_collisions list and the named 'home' pose [0, -1.57, 1.57, 1.57, 0] are worth copying out first (omx_f.srdf:32-38, 52-60).

There is no demonstration-recording layer anywhere in this repo -- physical_ai_tools is a README link, and nothing in the tree subscribes to an image topic and /joint_states together. For an imitation-learning capstone that is a whole missing package, and it is the one with the least existing scaffolding. Decide early whether the project records data or drives a scripted/pretrained policy; that choice changes the scope more than anything at the servo layer.

layers.name: Chunk buffer and time base
layers.whatItDoes: Holds the newest [16,10] chunk, knows how far into it wall-clock time has advanced, and swaps in a new chunk without discontinuity when inference finishes. Answers one question every tick: 'given it is now t seconds since this chunk's anchor, which two chunk steps do I sit between and what is the fraction?' Must survive a late chunk (keep extrapolating or freeze) and an early one (splice, don't jump).
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself. This is the one layer no vendor ships, because it encodes your policy's H, dt, anchor convention and replan cadence. ros2_control's JTC contains a version of it but tied to the FollowJointTrajectory action, not to a free-running policy.
layers.sizeEstimate: 60-90 lines, 4-8 hours including the edge cases. The naive version is 20 lines and is where the late-chunk and splice bugs live.
layers.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/chunk_executor_node.py lines 36-47 (PUBLISH_STEPS=8, EXECUTE_STEPS=3) and dummy_policy.py:23-24 (H=16, DT=0.04). Current replan period = EXECUTE_STEPS*DT*TIME_SCALE = 3*0.04*2.0 = 0.24 s = 4.17 Hz, publishing 8 of the 16 available steps.
layers.ifMissing: You get the current design: republish the whole segment every replan and let JTC re-time it. Works, but PUBLISH_STEPS/EXECUTE_STEPS exists only to hide JTC's zero-velocity-at-end rule, and the chunk's last 8 steps are thrown away every cycle.

layers.name: Decode and inverse kinematics
layers.whatItDoes: chunk[k] -> 6D rotation to R -> compose with anchor T -> 5-DOF projection -> analytic IK -> 5 joint angles + gripper width. Already built and validated to 3.4e-16 m.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself for a 5-DOF arm with a forced-yaw mechanism. No off-the-shelf IK knows that yaw = atan2(y, x-BASE_X) is a constraint rather than a DOF.
layers.sizeEstimate: Done. omx_kinematics.py is 216 lines, action_format.py is 192 lines.
layers.evidence: open_manipulator/docker/workspace/dummy_exec/omx_kinematics.py and action_format.py (decode_chunk at line 160, joints_to_T at line 70).
layers.ifMissing: Nothing to rebuild. This layer is finished and is the strongest part of the stack.

layers.name: Trajectory sampler (the spline)
layers.whatItDoes: Turns 25 Hz joint waypoints into a setpoint at whatever rate the servo loop runs. With positions+velocities this is a cubic Hermite per joint, evaluated at each tick. This is precisely what ros2_control's JointTrajectoryController was silently doing: linear if a point carries positions only, cubic if it carries positions+velocities, quintic if it also carries accelerations.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: usually-yourself once you leave ros2_control. The maths is textbook; the value JTC added was the bookkeeping around it, not the polynomial.
layers.sizeEstimate: 40 lines, 2-3 hours. build_segment() already computes the central-difference velocities the Hermite needs (chunk_executor_node.py:74-95), so the remaining work is literally the basis functions and an evaluate(t).
layers.evidence: https://control.ros.org/humble/doc/ros2_controllers/joint_trajectory_controller/doc/trajectory.html documents linear/cubic/quintic selection. Their own code comment at chunk_executor_node.py:38-47 already states this correctly. At 100 Hz each 0.04 s chunk step spans exactly 4 host ticks.
layers.ifMissing: Send chunk steps raw at 25 Hz and let the servo's own profile generator do the smoothing (Option A below). Legitimate, smaller, and the servo profile is a trapezoid rather than a spline - so joint-space motion is C1 but piecewise, and the end-effector path bows slightly between waypoints.

layers.name: Fixed-rate control loop (the clock)
layers.whatItDoes: The one thing that actually determines determinism: a loop that wakes at a fixed period, samples the spline, writes the bus, and does not drift. Plus a watchdog that freezes the last commanded position if no chunk arrives within N ms. ros2_control gave them this as update_rate: 100 in hardware_controller_manager.yaml.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself, and it is 20 lines that people get wrong in one specific way: sleep(period) accumulates drift; next_deadline += period then sleep(next_deadline - now) does not.
layers.sizeEstimate: 20 lines for the loop, plus ~15 lines of instrumentation (log perf_counter() into a preallocated array, dump p50/p95/p99/max at the end). Write the instrumentation on day one, not after something feels wrong.
layers.evidence: open_manipulator/open_manipulator_bringup/config/omx_f_follower_ai/hardware_controller_manager.yaml line 4: 'update_rate: 100  # Hz'. Same value in all 11 vendor variants.
layers.ifMissing: Timing jitter, which costs less than they fear: at 0.2 m/s end-effector speed, 1 ms = 0.20 mm, 5 ms = 1.00 mm, 10 ms = 2.00 mm. Their already-accepted 6.48 mm gravity droop is equivalent to 32 ms of jitter. CPython on a non-RT Jetson delivers p99 of 1-3 ms in a loop like this.

layers.name: Joint <-> tick conversion and limit clamping
layers.whatItDoes: radians to DYNAMIXEL pulses with a per-joint sign and zero offset, then clamps into the configured position limits before anything reaches the wire. This is the layer whose logic lived in the external package they could not read - it is not in the C++ at all, it is in the unit_multiplier/offset fields of the model files under /param/dxl_model that the DynamixelHardware plugin loads at startup.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself, and it is far smaller than its reputation. 4096 pulses/rev means 1 pulse = 0.087890625 deg = 0.0015339808 rad exactly. rad = (tick - 2048) * 2*pi/4096.
layers.sizeEstimate: 30 lines of arithmetic plus a one-off calibration script to find each joint's zero tick and sign. Budget half a day for the calibration, not the code.
layers.evidence: Resolution 4096 pulse/rev from https://emanual.robotis.com/docs/en/dxl/x/xl430-w250/ and https://docs.robotis.com/docs/dxl/model_reference/x_series/xl_series/xl330-m288/. The vendor's hard limits are in open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro: dxl12 Min 830 / Max 3129, dxl13 Min 1024 / Max 3140, dxl14 and dxl15 0..4095 (i.e. no limit), dxl11 and dxl16 none at all. Confirmation of the external indirection: dynamixel_hardware_interface.cpp calls dxl_comm_->OverrideUnitInfo(comm_id, id, data_name, unit_multiplier, is_signed, offset) and the xacro sets <param name="dynamixel_model_folder">/param/dxl_model</param>.
layers.ifMissing: You command the wrong joint into a hard stop. Note joint1 (id 11) is Operating Mode 4 = extended position, which wraps through multi-turn and has NO position limit configured - a sign error there does not hit a limit, it keeps going.

layers.name: Protocol 2.0 packet layer (Sync Write / Sync Read)
layers.whatItDoes: One Sync Write carrying all 6 goal positions, one Sync Read pulling all 6 present positions back. Their dxl_raw.py already has CRC, byte stuffing, packet build/parse and single-ID read/ping; what is missing is the group instructions 0x83 (Sync Write), 0x82 (Sync Read) and optionally 0x8A (Fast Sync Read).
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: off-the-shelf normally (DynamixelSDK), always-yourself in their case and it is a good trade - the packet format is 6 fields and they have already verified their CRC byte-for-byte against three published ROBOTIS example packets.
layers.sizeEstimate: 100 lines total: ~40 for Sync Write, ~60 for Sync Read including the 6-status-packet parse. 1 day. Fast Sync Read is another 30 lines and saves 320 us plus five bus turnarounds per cycle - skip it until you have measured that you need it.
layers.evidence: dxl_basics/dxl_raw.py - Bus.send/recv/txrx at lines 200-252, correct length semantics ('len(param) + 3') documented at line 20. Packet sizes derived from https://emanual.robotis.com/docs/en/dxl/protocol2/ : total = 10 + N params. SyncWrite 6x4B = 44 B, SyncRead request = 20 B, each status packet = 15 B.
layers.ifMissing: Six separate round trips instead of two. That is ~6x the wire time and 6x the USB round trips - it turns a 1.5 ms cycle into something like 15 ms and caps you near 60 Hz.

layers.name: Serial transport (termios / USB CDC)
layers.whatItDoes: Gets bytes onto /dev/ttyACM0 and back with a bounded timeout, and guarantees no second process is on the port. Already written as a 40-line stdlib termios backend so it needs neither pyserial nor the container.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: off-the-shelf normally (pyserial), and their from-scratch version is correct for ping/read but has one property that is fatal in a 100 Hz loop - see the finding on VTIME.
layers.sizeEstimate: Written. ~10 lines to change for control-loop use (select-based timeout) plus 3 lines for the exclusive lock.
layers.evidence: dxl_basics/dxl_raw.py:141-142 sets cc[VMIN]=0, cc[VTIME]=1. VTIME is in deciseconds, so 1 is the minimum non-zero value = 100 ms. _RawSerial.read() at line 158 loops on os.read, each call blocking up to that 100 ms. One silent servo therefore costs 100 ms = ten missed cycles at 100 Hz.
layers.ifMissing: The port is the single shared resource in this whole system and it already burned them once (the teammate's PWM experiment). fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) right after os.open is three lines and makes that entire bug class impossible.

layers.name: Servo register configuration (the init table)
layers.whatItDoes: Writes every non-default register at every boot: Drive Mode, Operating Mode, Return Delay Time, position limits, P/I/D gains, Profile Velocity, Profile Acceleration - then reads them all back and asserts they took. The vendor's hardware interface did this invisibly at on_init from the <param> tags in the xacro.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself. This is the layer that explains their 'RAM registers silently resetting on power cycle' mystery, and owning it explicitly is arguably the single biggest win of the whole rewrite.
layers.sizeEstimate: 60 lines plus a readback assertion. Half a day. The readback is the part everyone skips and the part that would have saved them weeks.
layers.evidence: omx_f.ros2_control.xacro gpio blocks for dxl11..dxl16. On X-series the EEPROM/RAM boundary is address 64 (first RAM register is Torque Enable(64)), confirmed at https://docs.robotis.com/docs/dxl/model_reference/x_series/xl_series/xl430-w250/. So Return Delay Time(9)=0, Drive Mode(10)=4, Operating Mode(11), Min/Max Position Limit(48/52) survive a power cycle; Position P/I/D Gain(80/82/84)=1000/0/1000, Profile Acceleration(108)=25 and Profile Velocity(112)=50 do NOT.
