layers.name: DYNAMIXEL internal profile generator (firmware)
layers.whatItDoes: Between your Goal Position write and the PID sits a trajectory generator. Drive Mode(10) bit 2 selects how it is parameterised. The vendor sets Drive Mode = 4, so bit 2 is SET: time-based profile. In that mode Profile Velocity(112) is the total profile time t3 in milliseconds and Profile Acceleration(108) is the acceleration time t1 in milliseconds, constrained to t1 <= t3/2. Writing a new Goal Position mid-profile regenerates the profile from the present position and velocity.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: vendor - it is in the servo firmware and you cannot change it, only parameterise it. But you must decide the parameters, and this is the design decision the whole question turns on.
layers.sizeEstimate: Zero lines. Two register values per servo, and one 20-minute experiment to choose them.
layers.evidence: omx_f.ros2_control.xacro: every servo has Drive Mode=4, Profile Velocity=50, Profile Acceleration=25. Time-based semantics from https://docs.robotis.com/docs/dxl/model_reference/x_series/xl_series/xl330-m288/ : 'Sets the time span to reach the velocity (the total time) of the Profile', unit 1 msec; 'Profile Acceleration(108, Acceleration time) will not exceed 50% of Profile Velocity(112)'. Time-based profile requires firmware V42+.
layers.ifMissing: Set PV=PA=0 and you get a step profile: Goal Position jumps instantly and the PID alone absorbs it. With 2 deg steps into a loop that saturates at 10 deg of error, that is near-full PWM for a few milliseconds per step - audible clacking, high peak current, and a staircase of 25 exponential settles per second.

layers.name: DYNAMIXEL position PID -> PWM (firmware)
layers.whatItDoes: Closes the position loop at roughly 1 kHz (ROBOTIS does not publish the figure; 1 kHz is their own stated 'reasonable frequency'). Error is Goal Position AFTER the profile generator minus Present Position, measured in pulses. Output is PWM, clipped to PWM Limit(36) = 885 units where 885 = 100% duty. Gains convert as KPP = P/128, KPI = I/65536, KPD = D/16. Feedforward 1st/2nd Gain(90/88) both default to 0 and the vendor leaves them there.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: vendor. You choose three numbers and otherwise cannot see inside it.
layers.sizeEstimate: Zero lines. Three register values, and the tuning is empirical.
layers.evidence: Gain conversions and PWM Limit 885 (unit 0.113%) from https://emanual.robotis.com/docs/en/dxl/x/xl430-w250/. Vendor values P=1000/I=0/D=1000 in omx_f.ros2_control.xacro. With P=1000, KPP = 7.8125 PWM per pulse, so the output saturates at 885/7.8125 = 113.3 pulses = 9.96 deg of error - beyond ~10 deg the loop is effectively bang-bang.
layers.ifMissing: Nothing to build, but I=0 has a direct measurable consequence: with no integral term there is nothing to null a constant gravity torque, which is exactly their 6.48 mm droop. The arithmetic closes: 6.48 mm at ~0.30 m reach = 0.0216 rad = 1.238 deg = 14.1 pulses; 14.1 x 7.8125 = 110 PWM = 12.4% duty, a plausible gravity hold. ROBOTIS's own older open_manipulator_x config uses I=100.

keyFindings: Drive Mode = 4 in omx_f.ros2_control.xacro sets bit 2, which means TIME-BASED profile. So 'Profile Velocity 50' is not a velocity - it is 50 milliseconds of total profile time, and 'Profile Acceleration 25' is 25 ms of acceleration time. Since t1 = t3/2 exactly, there is no constant-velocity segment: it is a pure triangular profile. Anyone reading those two numbers as rev/min will design the wrong system.

The ratio that matters is R = profile time / command period. Vendor OMX-F: 50 ms / 10 ms = 5. The servo therefore NEVER finishes a profile - every 10 ms it abandons the current triangle and regenerates from its present position and velocity toward the new goal. That is the invisible smoother that made the vendor stack feel good. ROBOTIS themselves vary it: open_manipulator_x uses PV=20/PA=10 (R=2), omy_l100 uses PV=10/PA=5 (R=1). There is no magic value.

Serial bus arithmetic at 1 Mbps, 8N1 (10 bits/byte = 10.0 us/byte exactly). Protocol 2.0 packet total = 10 + N_params bytes. Sync Write of 4-byte Goal Position to 6 servos: N = 2+2+6*5 = 34, total 44 B = 440 us. Sync Read request: N = 2+2+6 = 10, total 20 B = 200 us. Each status packet = 4+1+2+1+1+4+2 = 15 B = 150 us, x6 = 900 us. Read-then-write cycle = 200 + 900 + 440 = 1540 us -> theoretical ceiling 649 Hz. Fast Sync Read (0x8A) replaces the six status packets with one 58 B packet: cycle drops to 1220 us -> 820 Hz.

The bus is NOT the constraint and should not drive the design. Bus utilisation at 1540 us/cycle: 3.9% at 25 Hz, 15.4% at 100 Hz, 30.8% at 200 Hz, 77% at 500 Hz. Anything from 25 to 200 Hz has enormous margin. The real ceiling is USB CDC framing on /dev/ttyACM0 - full-speed USB schedules bulk transfers on 1 ms frames, so a write-then-read round trip costs 1-2 ms of pure scheduling on top of the 1.1 ms of wire time. Expect a measured cycle of 2.5-4 ms, i.e. 250-400 Hz. Raising baud to 4 Mbps cuts wire time 4x (1540 -> 385 us) but leaves the USB round trip untouched, so it buys almost nothing.

Return Delay Time(9) defaults to 250, and the unit is 2 us - that is 500 us per servo, 3000 us for six, nearly tripling the Sync Read cost. The vendor sets it to 0 on every servo. It lives at address 9, which is EEPROM, so it survives a power cycle - but only if someone wrote it once. Check it before blaming anything else for a slow loop.

The EEPROM/RAM boundary is address 64. Everything below 64 survives a power cycle; everything at 64 and above resets to firmware defaults. From the vendor's own config that means Return Delay Time(9), Drive Mode(10), Operating Mode(11) and the position limits(48/52) PERSIST, while Position P/I/D Gain(80/82/84), Profile Acceleration(108) and Profile Velocity(112) DO NOT. This is the complete explanation of the 'RAM registers silently resetting on power cycle' mystery.

After a power cycle without re-init the arm becomes two different robots. PV and PA both revert to 0 (step profile, zero smoothing), and the gains revert to per-family defaults that differ: XL430 (joints 1-3) to P=640/I=0/D=3600, XL330 (joints 4, 5, gripper) to P=400/I=0/D=0. The top half is heavily damped and the bottom half has no derivative term at all.

Their 6.48 mm gravity droop is a direct consequence of Position I Gain = 0, and the arithmetic closes exactly. 6.48 mm at ~0.30 m reach = 0.0216 rad = 1.238 deg = 14.1 pulses of position error. With P=1000, KPP = 1000/128 = 7.8125 PWM per pulse, so 14.1 pulses commands 110 PWM units out of the 885 limit = 12.4% duty - a plausible gravity hold. Two fixes: raise P (2000 halves the droop but also halves the 10 deg saturation band), or set I non-zero. ROBOTIS's own open_manipulator_x config uses I=100.

With P=1000, the position loop saturates at 885/7.8125 = 113.3 pulses = 9.96 degrees of error. Beyond about 10 degrees the PID is not a PID, it is bang-bang at full PWM. With the XL430 default P=640 that band is 15.6 deg; with the XL330 default P=400 it is 24.9 deg. This is the number that decides whether a large commanded jump is 'tracked' or 'thrown'.

They were never getting velocity feedforward from JointTrajectoryController. The config declares command_interfaces: [position] only (hardware_controller_manager.yaml). JTC applies feedforward and closed-loop PID only when a velocity or effort command interface exists; with position-only it is a pure open-loop passthrough that samples the spline and writes the position. The velocities in their messages shaped the spline but never reached the hardware. Dropping JTC costs them nothing here.

The ros2_control tag carries is_async="true" (omx_f.ros2_control.xacro line 4). In Jazzy this runs hardware read/write on a separate FIFO-scheduled thread triggered by the controller manager, so controllers see state that is one cycle old - a hidden 10 ms of latency at update_rate 100. A straightforward synchronous read-then-write loop is LOWER latency than what they had.

The PUBLISH_STEPS=8 / EXECUTE_STEPS=3 arrangement in chunk_executor_node.py exists purely to hide one JTC rule: allow_nonzero_velocity_at_trajectory_end defaults to false, so JTC rejects any trajectory whose final point has non-zero velocity. That is a controller policy, not physics. Owning the loop deletes the constraint entirely - a rolling buffer has no 'end' - and the whole publish-ahead-of-execute dance collapses into 'keep the buffer at least two chunks deep'. This is probably the single largest simplification available from the rewrite.

Jitter, converted into the only unit that matters here. At 0.2 m/s end-effector speed: 1 ms = 0.20 mm, 2 ms = 0.40 mm, 5 ms = 1.00 mm, 10 ms = 2.00 mm. Their measured 6.48 mm droop is equivalent to 32 ms of timing error. So any jitter under ~30 ms is smaller than an error they have already accepted. CPython on a non-RT Jetson in a deadline-based loop gives p50 of 0.1-0.3 ms and p99 of 1-3 ms - roughly 10x better than needed. Python is not the problem; the USB round trip (1-3 ms, and not jitter-free) dominates it.

dxl_raw.py sets cc[VMIN]=0, cc[VTIME]=1. VTIME is in DECISECONDS, so 1 is the smallest non-zero value = 100 ms, and each os.read() in _RawSerial.read() can block that long. One silent servo costs 100 ms, which is ten missed cycles at 100 Hz. Fine for s1_ping and s2_read; fatal in a control loop. Fix: VMIN=0, VTIME=0 plus select.select([fd], [], [], remaining), which takes a float timeout and can express 2 ms. About six lines.

Addresses 126, 128 and 132 are contiguous: 126 (2 bytes) + Present Velocity 128 (4 bytes) + Present Position 132 (4 bytes) = one 10-byte read. A single Sync Read from 126 returns all three per servo for 21 B per status packet, making the full cycle 1900 us / 526 Hz - still ample. But 126 is Present LOAD on XL430 (unit 0.1%) and Present CURRENT on XL330 (unit 1.0 mA). The same read address returns different physical quantities on the two halves of the arm.

Two ROBOTIS pages disagree on the XL430 Position D Gain default: emanual.robotis.com says 4,000 and docs.robotis.com says 3,600. This is exactly the class of problem that motivated the rewrite, and it has exactly one fix: read the register back from the servo and believe that.

Sync Write uses broadcast ID 0xFE and therefore returns no status packets at all - a failed write is silent. The only thing that verifies a write is the next read. If they want fault detection they must poll Hardware Error Status(70) explicitly, which can be folded in as a second Sync Read at ~1 Hz rather than every cycle.

The vendor's udev rule (open-manipulator-cdc.rules) is KERNEL=="ttyACM*", DRIVERS=="ftdi_sio", ATTR{device/latency_timer}="1". That matches ttyACM names but only under the ftdi_sio driver. If /dev/ttyACM0 is a genuine CDC-ACM device (OpenRB-150 / OpenCR, cdc_acm driver) the rule matches nothing and there is no latency_timer attribute to set. Worth one command to check: readlink /sys/class/tty/ttyACM0/device/driver.
tripwires: Two processes on one half-duplex bus will defeat every other precaution, and it has already happened to them once with the teammate's PWM experiment. fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) immediately after os.open in _RawSerial.__init__ is three lines and makes the entire failure mode impossible. Highest value-per-line item on the whole list - do it first.

Do not send sparse 25 Hz goals with Profile Velocity = 0. That combination is the worst of both worlds: 40 ms between setpoints with zero smoothing, so every step is a 2 deg jump into a loop that saturates at 10 deg. It will clack, spike current and look broken. If they go sparse, PV must be non-zero (~60-80 ms with PA = PV/2).

Do not send dense 100 Hz goals with the vendor's PV=50 either, unless they want the vendor's lag. R=5 means the servo is always aiming at a point 50 ms in the future. For dense commanding, PV around 15-20 ms at a 10 ms period (R = 1.5-2) keeps the missed-deadline protection while roughly halving the tracking lag.

EEPROM writes are REFUSED while Torque Enable(64) is 1, and the servo answers with error code 7 (access error) - which dxl_raw.py already decodes at ERRORS[7]. Any init sequence must be: torque off, EEPROM writes, RAM writes, torque on. Getting this order wrong produces a silent partial configuration.

EEPROM has finite write endurance (~100k cycles). An init routine that unconditionally rewrites Drive Mode, Operating Mode and the position limits on every launch is writing EEPROM several times a day for a semester. Read first, write only on mismatch. RAM registers can be written freely every boot and must be.

Never call print() inside the control loop. It costs 0.05-5 ms depending on whether stdout is a terminal or a pipe, which is larger than everything else in the loop combined, and it is the single most common cause of 'Python is too slow for real-time'. Log into a preallocated array and dump at the end.

The gripper (id 16) is Operating Mode 5 = current-based position control with Current Limit 600 and Goal Current 600, not plain position control. Commanding it like joints 1-5 will behave differently under contact - which is the whole point of mode 5, but only if they know it is there. It also has Shutdown = 21, a different fault mask from the other five.

joint1 (id 11) is Operating Mode 4 = extended position (multi-turn) and has NO Min/Max Position Limit configured, unlike joints 2 and 3. A sign error or a wrapped IK branch on joint1 does not hit a software limit - it keeps turning. joints 4 and 5 are set to 0..4095, which is the full range and therefore also no limit in practice. Only joints 2 and 3 are actually bounded (830..3129 and 1024..3140).

Measure the profile lag before believing any number for it, including mine. Whether a mid-profile Goal Position write regenerates from the present VELOCITY or from rest changes the steady-state lag by roughly 5x, and ROBOTIS does not document it. The experiment is 20 minutes: command a constant-velocity joint ramp, Sync Read Goal Position and Present Position every cycle, and read off the steady-state offset. Run it at PV=50/PA=25 and again at PV=0. That one measurement settles the entire sparse-vs-dense argument with their own data, and they can now run it precisely because they own the bus.

Instrument the loop period from day one, not after something feels wrong. Fifteen lines: log time.perf_counter() at the top of every iteration into a preallocated array, run 60 s at 100 Hz (6000 samples), print p50/p95/p99/max. If p99 < 3 ms and max < 20 ms, Python is settled and they never have to revisit it. Without this number the jitter question stays an anxiety instead of a fact.

Do not reach for PREEMPT_RT, SCHED_FIFO or a C++ rewrite to fix jitter at this stage. The USB round trip is the floor (1-3 ms) and it is identical in every language. os.sched_setscheduler with SCHED_FIFO is five lines and does help the tail, but only after everything else works - and it needs CAP_SYS_NICE, which is another container permission to argue with.

tcflush on every send() (dxl_raw.py:155, reset_input_buffer before each write) silently discards a status packet that is still arriving from the previous cycle. At 100 Hz that is usually the right behaviour, but it will mask a systematic one-cycle lag rather than reporting it. Count the discards and log the count, or a real bus problem will present as 'everything is fine, just slightly wrong'.

layers.name: Command sanity / rate gate (above IK)
layers.whatItDoes: Sits between the policy's [16,10] chunk and the IK. Rejects NaN and non-orthonormal 6D rotations, clamps per-tick joint delta to a velocity budget, and refuses a waypoint whose required joint speed exceeds the servo's Velocity Limit. At dt=0.04 s the XL430 ceiling is 265 x 0.229 rpm = 6.35 rad/s, i.e. 0.254 rad (14.6 deg) of joint travel per tick; anything above that the servo silently saturates and the arm falls behind the chunk without telling you.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself. No vendor ships this because it is policy-specific: it encodes your dt, your H, and your decoder's conventions. ros2_control's JointTrajectoryController does interpolation but no rejection.
layers.sizeEstimate: ~120 lines, 1-2 days including the test that feeds it a deliberately insane chunk. Cheap because it is pure math with no hardware in the loop.
layers.evidence: Velocity Limit 265 (0.229 rpm units) from XL430-W250 control table addr 44. Their decoder and dt=0.04/H=16 from the project brief. Vendor's only rate protection is Profile Velocity=50 in open_manipulator/open_manipulator_description/ros2_control/omx_f.ros2_control.xacro, which is a per-servo blend, not a rejection.
layers.ifMissing: A wrist singularity between two consecutive chunk steps demands a 180 deg joint5 flip in 40 ms (78 rad/s, 12x the limit). The servo goes at 6.35 rad/s instead, arrives 12 ticks late, and every downstream pose is wrong. Presents as 'the policy is bad', not as 'we saturated a joint'.

layers.name: Workspace + collision gate
layers.whatItDoes: Knows things the analytic IK structurally cannot: that z=0 is a table, that link6 can reach link0, and that the 5-DOF projection's yaw = atan2(y, x - BASE_X) is singular on the vertical line x = -11.25 mm, y = 0 (the joint1 axis itself, from the URDF joint1 origin -0.01125 0 0.034).
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: usually-yourself on a 5-DOF arm. MoveIt does it via FCL but you are not running MoveIt; you publish JointTrajectory straight to arm_controller, which does zero collision checking. ROBOTIS did write one (open_manipulator_collision, FCL capsules, 13 hard-coded pairs) but it is only launched from omy_l100_leader_ai.launch.py, subscribes to /leader/joint_states, defaults tip_link to rh_p12_rn_base (an OMY gripper that does not exist on OMX), and only publishes a std_msgs/Bool on /collision_flag that nothing on the follower consumes. On omx_f the vendor gave them nothing here.
layers.sizeEstimate: ~80-150 lines. A z-floor clamp is 5 lines. The 13 capsule pairs at ~10 lines each plus an FK reuse of code they already have is a day. A joint-space forbidden-box exclusion is cheaper and about as effective.
layers.evidence: open_manipulator_collision/src/self_collision_node.cpp lines 33-46 list the pairs: link6 vs link0/1/2/3, end_effector_flange_link vs link1/2/3/4, link5 vs link1/2/3, link4 vs link1, link3 vs link1. omx_f.srdf leaves 19 link pairs collision-enabled. omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py spawns only joint_state_broadcaster and arm_controller; gpio_command_controller is commented out at line 153.
layers.ifMissing: Two named things. (1) Table: the measured 6.48 mm droop means a commanded z of +5 mm is a real z of -1.5 mm; the servo then integrates PWM into the table forever. (2) The atan2 seam and the self-collision region are the SAME region of configuration space, because reaching x - BASE_X = 0 requires folding the arm back over itself. So one guard covers both.

layers.name: Calibration + software joint limits
layers.whatItDoes: Owns the tick<->radian map and clamps every target to limits set inside the firmware limits, which are themselves inside the mechanical stops. Also owns the gripper width map, which is a separate and much narrower range than the arm joints.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself, and this is the layer whose absence caused their original complaint. The 'tick-to-radian mapping that lives in an external C++ package' is almost certainly not a mystery algorithm: it is Homing Offset (addr 20, EEPROM, +/-1,044,479 pulses, default 0). Present Position already has it added. If ROBOTIS burned a nonzero value there, the CENTER=2048 hypothesis in their s2_read.py is wrong by exactly that amount.
layers.sizeEstimate: ~150 lines plus 3-4 hours of physical measurement with a protractor and torque off. The measurement, not the code, is the work.
layers.evidence: Three sources disagree, all in the repo. URDF omx_f.urdf gives every joint lower=-6.2832 upper=+6.2832 and effort=1000 N.m (the XL430 stall torque is 1.4 N.m, so the URDF is off by 714x). omx_f/joint_limits.yaml sets no position limits at all and max_velocity 5.0, which exceeds the URDF's own 4.8. The ros2_control xacro is the only source with real numbers: dxl12 830..3129 ticks = -107.05..+95.01 deg, dxl13 1024..3140 = -90.00..+95.98 deg, dxl14 and dxl15 0..4095 = no limit at all, dxl11 in Operating Mode 4 where limits are ignored by firmware, dxl16 in Mode 5 with no limits written. Gripper range appears only in open_manipulator_teleop/omx_f_teleop.py: gripper_min 0.0, gripper_max 1.1 rad = 717 of 4096 ticks; the SRDF says 1.0, the URDF says 6.28.
layers.ifMissing: Only 2 of 6 servos have any firmware position limit. The gripper has 3379 unguarded ticks of travel past its 717-tick linkage, and in Mode 5 it drives into that stop at Goal Current forever rather than faulting.

layers.name: Servo init, verify, and error-recovery state machine
layers.whatItDoes: The layer that does not exist yet in dxl_basics and is the single biggest source of 'more dangerous than the vendor stack'. On every boot AND after every servo reboot: ping, read Hardware Error Status (70), reboot if nonzero, torque off, write EEPROM, read every EEPROM register back, write RAM, read back, set Goal Position := Present Position, torque on, then arm Bus Watchdog.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: vendor normally. This is exactly what dynamixel_hardware_interface does on activate, driven by the <param> tags in the xacro, and it is the reason the vendor stack was survivable. It is also the part they cannot read, which is why they are rewriting.
layers.sizeEstimate: ~250-350 lines and the highest-risk week of the project. The write half is easy; the read-back-and-diff half is what earns its keep and is what everyone skips.
layers.evidence: omx_f.ros2_control.xacro sets disable_torque_at_init=true (line 25) precisely because EEPROM writes are refused with error 0x07 Access Error while Torque Enable=1. Registers it writes per servo: Drive Mode 4, Operating Mode 4/3/3/3/3/5, Return Delay Time 0 (factory default is 250 = 500 us), Position P Gain 1000, I 0, D 1000, Profile Velocity 50, Profile Acceleration 25, plus Min/Max Position Limit on 12/13 and Current Limit 600 / Goal Current 600 / Shutdown 21 on 16.
layers.ifMissing: Named registers that come back wrong after any power cycle or any post-overload reboot: Torque Enable (64) = 0, Profile Velocity (112) = 0 meaning INFINITE, Profile Acceleration (108) = 0 meaning infinite, Position P Gain (84) = 640 on XL430 and 400 on XL330 instead of 1000, Position D Gain (80) = 4000 on XL430 and 0 on XL330 instead of 1000, Goal Current (102) unset, Bus Watchdog (98) = 0, Hardware Error Status (70) cleared so yesterday's fault is invisible. Drive Mode 4 survives in EEPROM while Profile Velocity 50 does not survive in RAM, so you inherit time-based-profile semantics applied to a value of 0.

layers.name: Bus transport
layers.whatItDoes: Owns the port exclusively, batches the six goal writes into one Sync Write so all joints latch simultaneously, batches the reads into one Bulk/Sync Read, validates that the status packet's ID field matches the ID addressed, and never lets a timeout block the 40 ms loop.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: vendor normally (DynamixelSDK), and this is the part they have already built well. dxl_raw.py's CRC is verified byte-for-byte against three published ROBOTIS packets and the packet parse in recv() is correct.
layers.sizeEstimate: ~150 more lines on top of what exists: write (0x03), sync_write (0x83), bulk_read (0x92), reboot (0x08), TIOCEXCL, retry policy. 2-3 days.
layers.evidence: dxl_basics/dxl_raw.py currently implements only ping and read (lines 245-251); there is no write, no sync write, no bulk read, no port lock. Bus.__init__ uses timeout=0.1, so one silent servo costs 100 ms = 2.5 control periods. recv() at line 213 never checks raw[4] against the addressed ID. Sync Write (0x83) returns no status packets at all per Protocol 2.0, so it is both faster and simultaneity-correct.
layers.ifMissing: Six sequential round trips per tick on a USB CDC-ACM port, where the 1 ms USB frame quantization dominates the 1 Mbps line rate, costs 6-12 ms of the 40 ms budget before any timeout. One timeout costs 100 ms. The team's real exposure is that this presents as jitter and gets blamed on the policy.

layers.name: Servo firmware limits (inside the DYNAMIXEL)
layers.whatItDoes: The only guard that keeps working when the Jetson dies, the USB cable is pulled, or the Python process is SIGKILLed. Min/Max Position Limit (48/52) is enforced by firmware and refuses out-of-range goals. Current Limit (38) bounds Goal Current. Temperature Limit (31) and Shutdown (63) decide what the servo does to itself. Bus Watchdog (98) is the dead-man's switch.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: off-the-shelf (it is in the silicon), but YOU choose the values and they are worthless unless written and read back. The vendor wrote some of them and left large holes.
layers.sizeEstimate: Zero lines of logic, ~30 lines of register writes. The work is deciding the values and verifying the semantics, maybe 2 days including a deliberate kill -9 test.
layers.evidence: Position Limits are documented as not used in Extended Position Control Mode, so dxl11 (Mode 4) has none. Mode 5 supports -256..+256 rev, so dxl16 has none either. Shutdown 21 on the gripper = bits 0+2+4 (Input Voltage, Overheating, Electrical Shock) and deliberately CLEARS bit 5 Overload from the XL330 default of 53, because a current-based-position gripper is meant to stall on an object forever. Bus Watchdog is proven in this same repo: omy_f3m_current.ros2_control.xacro sets it to 1 (=20 ms) on all six servos. It is not set anywhere in omx_f.
layers.ifMissing: With no Bus Watchdog, a killed process leaves the arm holding its last Goal Position at 24% PWM duty on joint2 indefinitely; if that goal was into the table it stalls until Overload trips, torque cuts, and the arm falls. With Bus Watchdog set, the servo goes to state -1, applies Profile Acceleration and Profile Velocity as 0, makes goal values read-only, and freezes in place. Freeze beats drop on an arm that droops.

layers.name: Mechanical reality
layers.whatItDoes: The hard stops, the 12 V/5 V rails, the daisy-chain cable routing, gravity, and the table. It is the only layer that cannot be edited and the only one that enforces itself destructively.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: nobody writes it; you measure it. The 3-4 hours of protractor work is the highest-value-per-hour task on the whole list, because every electronic limit above it is a guess until you have done it.
layers.sizeEstimate: 3-4 hours of measurement, ~20 lines of constants. Plus one afternoon of cable-routing so joint1 cannot wind the harness.
layers.evidence: URDF link masses give 0.2689 kg distal to joint2 over a 340.7 mm reach to the finger root. Worst-case (fully horizontal) gravity torque computes to 0.579 N.m at joint2 and 0.278 N.m at joint3, i.e. 41.4% and 19.9% of the XL430-W250's 1.4 N.m stall torque. Their measured pose (0.333 / 0.248 N.m) is 58% and 89% of those worst cases. The link2->link3 vector is (0.0415, 0, 0.11315), a 120.5 mm link at a 20.14 deg offset, which is why the two joints load so differently.
layers.ifMissing: Their 6.48 mm droop was NOT measured at the worst pose. Scaling linearly with joint2 torque, full horizontal extension gives roughly 11.3 mm. Any z-floor margin sized on 6.48 mm is under-sized by ~75% exactly where the arm is most extended, which is where a UMI reach-and-grasp ends.

keyFindings: RANK 1, fix today, 2 lines: two processes on /dev/ttyACM0. This already happened to them once and nothing has changed since. Likelihood certain. Normal severity is hours of phantom debugging; worst case is a corrupted Goal Position write that passes CRC-16 (1 in 65536 per corrupted packet, and at 25 Hz x 6 joints that is once every ~7 minutes of corruption), producing a joint jump nobody can reproduce. Cheapest mitigation: fcntl.ioctl(fd, termios.TIOCEXCL) immediately after open in _RawSerial.__init__ (turns silent corruption into a clean EBUSY for the second opener, works across the Docker boundary because it is the same kernel inode), plus one line in Bus.txrx validating raw[4] == dxl_id. Note the vendor's own repo has this bug class: omx_f.ros2_control.xacro defaults port_name to /dev/ttyACM1 while omx_f_follower_ai.launch.py defaults it to /dev/ttyACM0.

RANK 2, the concrete RAM-reset scenario: on power-up the servos come back with Torque Enable (64) = 0, Profile Velocity (112) = 0, Profile Acceleration (108) = 0, Position P Gain (84) = 640 on the XL430s and 400 on the XL330s, Position D Gain (80) = 4000 on XL430 and 0 on XL330, Bus Watchdog (98) = 0, Hardware Error Status (70) cleared. But Drive Mode = 4 SURVIVES in EEPROM, as do Min/Max Position Limit, Current Limit, and Shutdown. Per the e-manual, 0 in the profile registers means infinite. So a driver that writes only Torque Enable and Goal Position produces: (a) a torque-on snap to whatever stale Goal Position is in RAM, executed at the 6.35 rad/s velocity limit while the arm is drooped; (b) every subsequent 40 ms chunk step delivered as an unprofiled slam instead of the vendor's 50 ms blend; (c) droop rising from 6.48 mm to about 10.1 mm on joints 1-3 (6.48 x 1000/640) and joints 4-5 running 2.5x softer with zero damping. It is MORE dangerous than the vendor stack specifically because the vendor's hardware interface reads its params back and refuses to activate, while a write-only driver starts happily and moves fast. Named registers to write and verify every boot: 10, 11, 20, 31, 38, 48, 52, 63, 64, 80, 82, 84, 98, 102, 108, 112.

The sharpest version of the RAM trap is not the power cycle, which you would notice, but the REBOOT. Recovering a servo from Overload requires instruction 0x08 Reboot (toggling Torque Enable does not clear Hardware Error Status on X-series), and Reboot resets the entire RAM area. So an overload at 3 a.m. during data collection silently reverts joint2 to Kp=640, Profile Velocity=0, and no Bus Watchdog, mid-run, with no power cycle to blame it on. Any recovery path in the driver must re-run the full RAM init, not just re-enable torque.

RANK 3, the only failure mode that reliably kills a servo: the gripper. XL330-M288 Current Limit (38) default is 1750 mA against a 1470 mA stall current and 0.52 N.m stall torque; the vendor writes 600. Goal Current (102) is RAM and resets; Current Limit is EEPROM and survives. Losing Goal Current gives up to 1470/600 = 2.45x grip force. Worse, the vendor sets Shutdown (63) = 21 on dxl16, which clears bit 5 (Overload) from the XL330 default of 53 - deliberately, because a current-based-position gripper is supposed to stall on an object indefinitely. Inherit that value and you have disabled the servo's own overload protection; the only thing left is Overheating at the Temperature Limit. Combine that with the gripper's real travel being 0.0 to 1.1 rad (717 of 4096 ticks, from open_manipulator_teleop/omx_f_teleop.py gripper_max=1.1, which the SRDF contradicts with 1.0 and the URDF contradicts with 6.28) and a width-mapping bug drives the linkage into its stop at full current until the motor cooks. Mitigation: write Current Limit 600 to EEPROM and Goal Current 600 to RAM every boot, clamp width to [0, 717] ticks, and poll Present Temperature (146) once a second since you have disabled the automatic guard.

RANK 4, torque transitions. Torque Disable is not 'safe shutdown', it is 'drop the arm': 0.2689 kg falls from up to 340.7 mm of reach. It is not dangerous to a person and it will not hurt the XL430s, but it breaks gripper fingers (link6/link7 are 12.1 g parts on an XL330) and whatever is on the table. Torque Enable is the mirror image: the servo starts tracking Goal Position (116), whose power-on initial value the e-manual lists as unspecified, so if the arm drooped or was moved by hand the full error is corrected at 6.35 rad/s. The fix is three lines and it is the same fix for both: read Present Position (132) on all six and write it to Goal Position (116) BEFORE writing Torque Enable = 1. Correct init order: open+TIOCEXCL -> ping -> read reg 70 -> reboot if nonzero -> torque OFF -> write EEPROM -> read EEPROM back -> write RAM -> read RAM back -> Goal := Present -> torque ON -> arm Bus Watchdog last. Correct shutdown order: command Present Position for a few ticks -> ramp to a folded rest pose -> write Bus Watchdog 0 -> and then LEAVE TORQUE ON. Only torque-off when a human needs to move it by hand, and only from the rest pose.

RANK 5, process killed mid-motion: nothing happens, and that is the problem. The servos are position servos with a setpoint; no packet arriving is not an event they react to. Three sub-cases. (a) Reachable last goal: the arm freezes holding 0.333 N.m at joint2, which computes to 211/885 = 24% PWM duty continuously, and heats toward the 72 C Temperature Limit over hours. (b) Last goal into the table or into itself: full-PWM stall until Overload trips (~5 s for the joints that still have Shutdown bit 5), torque cuts, arm falls. (c) SIGKILL during the torque-off window of init: limp, immediate drop. atexit and signal handlers cover SIGINT and SIGTERM only - not SIGKILL, not OOM, not a yanked USB cable. The answer is Bus Watchdog (98), RAM, 20 ms units, range 1-127: on timeout the servo sets itself to -1, applies Profile Acceleration and Profile Velocity as 0, stops, and makes goal values read-only until you write 0 back. It freezes rather than drops, which is the correct behavior for an arm with 6.48 mm of droop. ROBOTIS use it at value 1 (20 ms) on all six servos in omy_f3m_current.ros2_control.xacro but set it nowhere in omx_f. Honest caveat: that precedent is a current-control arm, and the e-manual does not explicitly confirm useful behavior in Position Control Mode. This is a 20-minute experiment (set 98 = 5, start a slow move, kill -9, watch) and it determines the entire safety story, so run it before building anything on top of it.

Corollary that surprises people: a physical e-stop that cuts the 12 V rail is a WORSE safety device on this arm than Bus Watchdog, because cutting power is exactly the torque-disable drop. On a droopy arm the safe failure is 'freeze', and only the servo firmware can deliver that.

Authority order for joint limits, from binding to advisory: (1) mechanical stops - unenforced by anything, enforced destructively by themselves; (2) Min/Max Position Limit (48/52) in servo EEPROM - the ONLY electronically enforced limit, survives a host crash, but applies only in Operating Mode 3, so dxl11 (Mode 4) and dxl16 (Mode 5) have none, and dxl14/dxl15 are written to 0..4095 which is no limit at all; (3) host software clamp - fastest and can express coupled limits, but dies with the process; (4) URDF and joint_limits.yaml - documentation only, and in this repo actively wrong (every joint +/-2pi, effort 1000 N.m against a 1.4 N.m stall). Belt and braces: measure the mechanics by hand, write EEPROM limits a few degrees inside that, clamp in software a few degrees inside THAT, put joint1 in Mode 3 unless multi-turn is genuinely needed, and read back every EEPROM write because a write attempted with torque on is refused with Protocol 2.0 error 0x07 Access Error and changes nothing.

What a 5-DOF analytic IK does not protect against, in descending order of how often it will actually bite: the table (a UMI policy works at the surface, and 6.48 mm of droop turns a commanded z=+5 mm into a real z=-1.5 mm); per-tick joint velocity (IK maps a point, not a rate - two consecutive chunk steps across a wrist singularity demand 78 rad/s at joint5, 12x the limit); the yaw seam at x = -11.25 mm, y = 0 where atan2(y, x - BASE_X) flips; self-collision; and objects not in the URDF at all (camera, mount, cabling). Useful geometric fact: the atan2 seam and the self-collision region are the same region of configuration space, because reaching the joint1 axis requires folding the arm back onto itself, so one guard covers both.

Yes, this arm can hit itself, and ROBOTIS have published exactly which pairs: open_manipulator_collision/src/self_collision_node.cpp lines 33-46 hard-code 13 pairs including link6 (a gripper finger) against link0, link1, link2 and link3. The SRDF independently leaves 19 link pairs collision-enabled and disables link6-link7 with reason 'Always', meaning ROBOTIS gave up modeling finger-against-finger entirely. Be honest about the ledger though: the vendor stack gave this team ZERO self-collision protection on omx_f. self_collision_node is launched only from omy_l100_leader_ai.launch.py, subscribes to /leader/joint_states, defaults tip_link to rh_p12_rn_base (an OMY part absent from the OMX), publishes only a Bool that nothing on the follower consumes, and falls back to a 2 cm x 20 cm capsule for every link because the URDF collision geometry is STL meshes, not cylinders. They lose nothing here by going from scratch - but they also gain nothing automatically.

How a servo reports distress, end to end: it sets the bit in Hardware Error Status (70) - bit 0 Input Voltage, bit 2 Overheating, bit 4 Electrical Shock, bit 5 Overload - and sets bit 7 (Alert) in the Error field of EVERY subsequent status packet. If the corresponding bit is also set in Shutdown (63), it sets Torque Enable to 0 on its own and blinks the LED at ~1 Hz. It keeps ANSWERING packets the whole time, so 'a servo that stops answering' is never the shutdown case. The host must: read reg 70 at least once a second, treat Alert as a first-class event, send Reboot (0x08) to clear, and then re-run the entire RAM init because Reboot wiped it. Their existing s2_read.py has a real bug here: `row[name] = D.to_int(data, signed) if err == 0` treats Alert (0x80 = 128) as a failed read, so the moment any servo has a hardware error every register prints '-' and the script says 'every read failed -- run s1_ping.py first' while the bus is perfectly healthy. Split it: alert = err & 0x80, code = err & 0x7F, and only code != 0 is a transport failure.

Diagnostic rule worth writing on the wall: the bus is a daisy chain, so if ids 14, 15 and 16 all go silent at once, the cable between 13 and 14 is loose - it is one connector, not three dead servos. The other clustered-failure mode is the power rails: the XL430s run at 11.1-12 V and the XL330s at 5 V, so a 5 V brownout drops 14/15/16 together and the XL330s log Input Voltage Error (bit 0), which the vendor's Shutdown 21 on the gripper explicitly includes - so the gripper torques off and releases the object while the arm keeps moving.

Their s2_read.py reads 13 registers. The 11 missing ones are all safety-relevant and cost about 15 minutes to add to a script they have already written: Firmware Version (6, decides whether Startup Configuration is even available - it needs V45+), Return Delay Time (9, factory default 250 = 500 us x 6 servos = 3 ms per tick of pure waste), Homing Offset (20, the likely answer to the tick-to-radian mystery), Temperature Limit (31), Current Limit (38), Velocity Limit (44), Startup Configuration (60), Shutdown (63), Hardware Error Status (70), Bus Watchdog (98), Goal Current (102), Present Input Voltage (144), Present Temperature (146). Read Homing Offset first: if it is nonzero, the CENTER=2048 hypothesis in their script is wrong by exactly that many ticks and the external C++ package's mapping is not a mystery algorithm, it is address 20.

Startup Configuration (60, EEPROM, firmware V45+) is the one register that directly attacks the RAM trap: bit 0 = Torque On at startup, bit 1 = restore the RAM area from backup at startup. Worth knowing it exists and worth checking Firmware Version (6) to see if their units support it. Do not rely on it: the init routine has to exist anyway for the reboot-after-overload path, which no startup setting covers. And bit 0 (torque on at startup) is actively hazardous on this arm unless Goal Position is known good, since it removes the operator from the torque-on transition entirely.
tripwires: The Drive Mode semantic flip, which will cost weeks and damage nothing. The vendor writes Drive Mode = 4, i.e. bit 2 set = TIME-BASED profile, in which Profile Velocity (112) means total move time in ms and Profile Acceleration (108) means acceleration time in ms. So the vendor's 50 and 25 mean a 50 ms move blended over a 25 ms accel ramp - deliberately just longer than their 40 ms tick, so consecutive chunk steps overlap and blend. With Drive Mode = 0 (the factory default, velocity-based) the SAME value 50 means 50 x 0.229 = 11.45 rpm = 1.2 rad/s, a 5x speed cap. A from-scratch driver that copies '50' without copying '4' produces an arm that lags every chunk and never reaches a waypoint. It will look exactly like a policy that does not work. Read Drive Mode bit 2 and branch on it explicitly; do not copy magic numbers across a semantic boundary.

Drive Mode bit 3 (value 8) is 'Torque On by Goal Update'. If anyone ever writes Drive Mode 12 instead of 4, the arm torques on the instant a Goal Position is written, with no explicit Torque Enable and therefore no chance to run the Goal := Present step first. That is the torque-on snap with the safety step structurally unreachable.

The 6.48 mm droop figure is being used as if it were a worst case and it is not. Their pose loads joint2 at 0.333 N.m against a computed worst case of 0.579 N.m (58%) and joint3 at 0.248 against 0.278 (89%). Scaling droop linearly with joint2 torque gives roughly 11.3 mm at full horizontal extension. Any table-clearance margin sized on 6.48 mm is undersized by about 75% precisely at full reach, which is where a UMI grasp ends.

Everything in the configuration layer fails by looking like a bad policy. Wrong gains present as droop and ringing. Wrong profile semantics present as lag. A 100 ms read timeout on one flaky servo presents as jitter. The Alert bit misread presents as 'the bus is down'. This is the same failure they already suffered with the vendor stack, and rewriting from scratch does not fix it by itself - it fixes it only if they add read-back-and-diff on every register they write, and log a per-tick record of commanded vs present position. That logging is maybe 40 lines and it is the difference between the rewrite paying off and the rewrite reproducing the original problem with their own code.

The 0.1 s default timeout in Bus.__init__ is 2.5 control periods. With six sequential reads per tick, one intermittently slow servo turns a 40 ms loop into 140 ms without raising any error anywhere. Drop it to ~10 ms (a 1 Mbps round trip is under 1 ms of line time, but USB CDC-ACM adds 1 ms frame quantization, so 10 ms is roughly 5x margin), count timeouts in a counter you actually print, and move to Sync Write (0x83, no status packets returned at all) plus Bulk Read (0x92) so there is one deadline per tick instead of twelve. Sync Write also fixes a real correctness issue nobody notices: six separate writes spread over ~5 ms mean the six joints start at six different times.

Joint1 is in Operating Mode 4 (Extended Position), where the e-manual states Min/Max Position Limit are not used. That is 512 revolutions of unguarded travel on the joint that carries the entire daisy-chain harness. Cable wind-up will tear the wiring out, and it is silent until it is catastrophic. Unless multi-turn base yaw is genuinely required, put joint1 in Mode 3 and write measured limits. If Mode 4 is required, the limit has to live in the host clamp and the host clamp has to survive a restart, which means persisting the unwrapped turn count somewhere.

dxl14 and dxl15 are configured Min 0 / Max 4095, which reads like a limit and is not one - it is the full range. The wrist can be driven into the forearm with the firmware's full blessing. Measure the real travel by hand with torque off before writing anything.

Do not blanket-copy Shutdown = 21 from the gripper to the arm joints. On dxl16 it is a considered trade (hold the object, accept the heat risk) that only makes sense for a current-based-position gripper. Applied to joint2 or joint3 it disables the one automatic guard that stops a stalled joint from cooking itself against the table. Conversely, if the gripper keeps the XL330 default of 53, it will trip Overload and DROP the object mid-task - which is why ROBOTIS changed it. Whichever you pick, you have chosen a failure mode; pick it deliberately and write the reason in a comment.

Order of operations that bites everyone once: arming Bus Watchdog before the init sequence finishes makes the watchdog trip during your own setup, and since a tripped watchdog makes goal values read-only, the driver then appears to be writing goals that do nothing. Arm it last, immediately before the control loop starts, and disarm it (write 0 to 98) before any deliberate pause.

Honest ranking of what actually destroys hardware versus what only destroys time. Destroys hardware: the gripper stalling at up to 1470 mA with Overload shutdown cleared (this one reliably kills an XL330-M288); joint1 winding the harness in Extended Position Mode; driving into a mechanical stop at 6.35 rad/s, which strips the XL430-W250's plastic gearset; and the torque-disable drop, which breaks the 12 g gripper fingers rather than the servos. Destroys only time, but a lot of it: wrong gains, wrong profile semantics, read timeouts, the Alert-bit misread, and post-reboot RAM loss. The uncomfortable truth is that the time-destroying list is where they will actually lose the capstone, and the vendor stack was not protecting them from any of it.

layers.name: Policy + chunk semantics
layers.whatItDoes: Emits the [H,10] tensor and defines what the numbers mean: delta position, 6D rotation, absolute gripper width, relative to an anchor. Owns H, dt, and the normalisation stats.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: off-the-shelf — every project in this survey takes the policy from a library (LeRobot policies, ACT, diffusion_policy, openpi) and writes only the config. Nobody hand-rolls the network for a capstone.
layers.sizeEstimate: ~0 new lines if you use a library policy. For reference, LeRobot's ACT config is one dataclass; the only fields that matter operationally are chunk_size/n_action_steps.
layers.evidence: lerobot src/lerobot/policies/act/configuration_act.py: chunk_size=100, n_action_steps=100, temporal_ensemble_coeff=None (off). diffusion: horizon=64, n_action_steps=32. smolvla/pi0: chunk_size=50, n_action_steps=50. Their H=16 @ dt=0.04 = 0.64 s of open loop, which is SHORTER than every library default (ACT 3.3 s @30 Hz, pi0 1.0 s @50 Hz).
layers.ifMissing: Nothing to deploy.

layers.name: Chunk scheduler / action queue
layers.whatItDoes: Decides when to re-infer, what to do with overlapping predictions from consecutive chunks, and how to compensate for inference + actuation latency. This is the layer that turns 'a chunk arrived' into 'one command is due right now'.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: usually-yourself, but from one of exactly three published patterns. Everyone re-implements it because it is ~100-300 lines and couples to their own timing.
layers.sizeEstimate: 80-300 lines. Measured: lerobot ActionChunkBroker equivalent in openpi is trivial; lerobot's async robot_client.py is 530 lines (includes gRPC); lerobot's RTC engine is 602 lines; UMI does it inline in eval_real.py in ~40 lines (eval_real.py lines 501-527).
layers.evidence: Three patterns, all verified in source: (1) OPEN-LOOP REPLAY — tonyzhaozh/act imitate_episodes.py:248 `if t % query_frequency == 0` with query_frequency = chunk_size, and openpi examples/aloha_real/main.py action_horizon=25 @ max_hz=50. (2) TEMPORAL ENSEMBLING — act/imitate_episodes.py:250-259, k=0.01 exponential weights over all chunks that predicted this timestep. (3) TIMESTAMPED SCHEDULING — universal_manipulation_interface/eval_real.py:502-520 stamps every action with `np.arange(len(action))*dt + obs_timestamps[-1]`, drops actions already in the past (`is_new = action_timestamps > curr_time + 0.01`), and submits the rest. lerobot's async path uses chunk_size_threshold=0.5 and aggregate_fn_name=weighted_average (robot_client.py:29-31, 237-280).
layers.ifMissing: Either you re-infer every tick and throw away 15 of 16 predictions (works, wastes GPU, and is what LeRobot's default sync engine effectively does at n_action_steps=1), or you replay chunks blind and get a visible discontinuity at every chunk boundary.

layers.name: Anchor / relative-action handling
layers.whatItDoes: Converts anchor-relative deltas into absolute targets. Must decide WHICH state the anchor is taken from, and must keep that anchor fixed for the whole chunk rather than refreshing it per tick.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself, and it is the single most likely place to lose a week. LeRobot has this exact problem written down as a known unsupported case.
layers.sizeEstimate: 30-80 lines, but the debugging is the cost, not the code. LeRobot needed a dedicated `reanchor_relative_rtc_prefix` helper plus a `RelativeActionsProcessorStep` with cached state to get it right.
layers.evidence: lerobot src/lerobot/rollout/inference/sync.py lines 36-47, verbatim: "The per-tick flow refreshes ``RelativeActionsProcessorStep._last_state`` every call, so cached chunk actions popped on later ticks get reanchored to the *current* robot state and absolute targets drift through the chunk. Relative-action policies are rejected at context-build time today; RTC postprocesses the whole chunk and is unaffected." LeRobot's SYNCHRONOUS engine REFUSES to run relative-action policies. Only the RTC engine (src/lerobot/rollout/inference/rtc.py, 602 lines, lines 234-249 and 483-493) handles them, via explicit re-anchoring. UMI sidesteps it entirely by converting to absolute in `get_real_umi_action` before the chunk ever reaches the env (eval_real.py:481).
layers.ifMissing: Silent drift within each chunk. The robot appears to work, then creeps — worst possible failure mode because it looks like a policy quality problem.

layers.name: Task-space to joint-space (IK, projection, workspace guard)
layers.whatItDoes: Turns an EE pose into 5 joint angles, projects away the DOF the mechanism cannot express, clips to a workspace box, and rate-limits EE jumps.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: always-yourself for a non-standard arm. LeRobot ships one only for SO-100/SO-101, and it is the largest single file in their robot layer.
layers.sizeEstimate: 400-650 lines. Measured: lerobot src/lerobot/robots/so_follower/robot_kinematic_processor.py is 648 raw / 504 sloc, split into EEReferenceAndDelta, EEBoundsAndSafety, InverseKinematicsEEToJoints, GripperVelocityToJoint, and forward-kinematics observation steps. The team has already built the FK/IK core (validated to 3.4e-16 m), so realistically 150-250 lines remain for the bounds/rate-limit/processor plumbing.
layers.evidence: lerobot robot_kinematic_processor.py lines 192-264: EEBoundsAndSafety clips position to a box and rate-limits per-frame steps with `max_ee_step_m: float = 0.05` — at 30 Hz that is a 1.5 m/s cap. layers.name: Rate adaptation / interpolation (policy Hz -> command Hz)
layers.whatItDoes: Bridges the gap between the policy tick and the rate at which the actuator wants setpoints.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: Split down the middle, and the split is the most interesting finding in this research. Position-servo projects (LeRobot, ALOHA) DO NOT interpolate. Industrial-arm projects (UMI, Diffusion Policy) build a dedicated interpolating process.
layers.sizeEstimate: LeRobot: 136 raw / 102 sloc (src/lerobot/utils/action_interpolator.py), pure linear lerp, and DISABLED BY DEFAULT (interpolation_multiplier: int = 1). UMI: 208 lines of SE(3) PoseTrajectoryInterpolator + a 375-line RTDEPositionalController process + 219+187 lines of shared-memory ring buffer/queue to talk to it = ~990 lines.
layers.evidence: lerobot src/lerobot/rollout/configs.py:310-315: "Robot commands sent per policy action. Values > 1 linearly interpolate between consecutive policy actions for smoother motion: commands go to the robot at ``fps × multiplier`` Hz while policy inference and dataset recording stay at ``fps`` Hz." Default 1. Contrast universal_manipulation_interface/umi/real_world/rtde_interpolation_controller.py:33-35 (frequency=125, lookahead_time=0.1, gain=300) and franka_interpolation_controller.py:80 (frequency=1000, Kx=[750,750,750,15,15,15]). layers.ifMissing: On a DYNAMIXEL at 25-30 Hz: nothing, if you use the servo profile (next layer). On a UR5 at 10 Hz: the arm stutters visibly, which is exactly why UMI built the 125 Hz process.

layers.name: Robot facade (get_observation / send_action)

layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: usually-yourself, but it is astonishingly small — and for THIS EXACT ARM it already exists.
layers.sizeEstimate: 165-250 lines. Measured: lerobot src/lerobot/robots/omx_follower/omx_follower.py = 231 raw / 164 sloc. ROBOTIS' own fork version = 273 raw. so_follower.py = 242, koch_follower.py = 248. The abstract contract (src/lerobot/robots/robot.py, 211 lines) has 9 members, of which exactly TWO are in the hot loop.

layers.name: Register provisioning / calibration recipe
layers.whatItDoes: Writes the operating modes, PID gains, profile settings, position limits, current limits and shutdown mask into each servo at every connect, and establishes one authoritative source for tick<->radian and for joint limits.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: usually-yourself — and this is where all four of the team's unexplained problems actually live. For the OMX the authoritative recipe is 40 lines and is published.
layers.sizeEstimate: 40-60 lines of writes, plus a calibration routine. LeRobot's generic calibration helpers (set_half_turn_homings + record_ranges_of_motion) live in motors_bus.py lines 775-840, ~70 lines.
layers.evidence: THE ANSWER TO THEIR 'THREE SOURCES DISAGREE' PROBLEM. ROBOTIS-GIT/lerobot branch feature-omx-devel, src/lerobot/robots/omx_follower/omx_follower.py lines 166-208, configure(): Operating_Mode — shoulder_pan(11)=4 EXTENDED_POSITION, joints 12/13/14/15=3 POSITION, gripper(16)=5 CURRENT_BASED_POSITION. Then for ALL motors: Return_Delay_Time=0, Drive_Mode=4, Position_P_Gain=1000, Position_I_Gain=0, Position_D_Gain=1000, Profile_Velocity=50, Profile_Acceleration=25. Joint limits in RAW TICKS: shoulder_lift 830..3129; elbow_flex 1024..3140; wrist_flex 0..4095; wrist_roll 0..4095 (shoulder_pan deliberately unlimited because it is in extended-position mode). Gripper: Current_Limit=600, Goal_Current=600, Shutdown=21 (=1 input-voltage + 4 overheating + 16 electrical-shock). THE TICK MAPPING they could not read: ROBOTIS-GIT/dynamixel_hardware_interface, param/dxl_model/xl430_w250.model, a plain 5-column text file — `Present Position  0.0015339807878856412  rad  signed  -3.14159265359`. That constant is exactly 2*pi/4096. So rad = tick*2*pi/4096 - pi, i.e. tick 2048 = 0 rad. Same file gives Present Velocity = 0.0239691227 rad/s per unit. There are 110 such .model files in that repo. WHY RAM RESETS: per the ROBOTIS e-manual, XL430-W250 EEPROM is addresses 0-63 and RAM is 64-661. Position D/I/P Gain (80/82/84), Profile Acceleration (108), Profile Velocity (112) and Torque Enable (64) are all RAM — they reset on every power cycle by design. Defaults XL430: P=640 I=0 D=4000; XL330: P=400 I=0 D=0. Both models have Startup Configuration at EEPROM address 60 (initial 0, range 0-3): bit 0 = Startup Torque On, bit 1 = "On startup, use the backup data to restore the RAM area" (XL330 requires firmware V46+).
layers.ifMissing: Exactly what they experienced: limits that disagree between the URDF, the ros2_control xacro and the servo EEPROM; gains that silently revert; a tick mapping nobody can find.

layers.name: Motor bus (sync_read / sync_write / register tables)
layers.whatItDoes: One sync_read for all 6 present positions, one sync_write for all 6 goal positions, per-model control-table address lookup, normalisation, retries, and sole ownership of the serial port.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: off-the-shelf in every single project surveyed. Nobody writes this from scratch; they write a thin typed wrapper over the vendor SDK.
layers.sizeEstimate: LeRobot's wrapper: motors_bus.py 1296 raw / 1067 sloc + dynamixel/dynamixel.py 264/179 + dynamixel/tables.py 217/163 + encoding_utils.py 67/41 = ~1844 raw / 1450 sloc, and it sits ON TOP of dynamixel_sdk. A minimal version for one arm with fixed models is realistically 250-400 lines.
layers.evidence: THIS IS THE REAL GAP IN THEIR CURRENT CODE. dxl_basics/dxl_raw.py (288 raw / 202 sloc) implements crc16, stuff/unstuff, _RawSerial (termios), Bus.send, Bus.recv, Bus.txrx, Bus.ping and Bus.read — there is no write(), no sync_read(), no sync_write(). Bus timing at 1 Mbps 8N1, computed from the Protocol 2.0 frame (10 bytes overhead + params): sync_write Goal_Position to 6 servos = 44 bytes = 440 us, no status packets. sync_read Present_Position from 6 = 20-byte instruction (200 us) + 6x15-byte status (900 us) = ~1.11 ms with Return_Delay_Time=0, but ~4.10 ms at the factory default of 250 (=500 us each). One read+write tick: 1.55 ms configured vs 4.54 ms factory. Doing the same reads one register at a time (the s2_read.py pattern) costs 21 ms for 12 registers at RDT=0 and 57 ms at the factory default. Vendor SDK size for the protocol-2 path only: protocol2_packet_handler.py 789, port_handler.py 136, group_sync_read.py 145, group_sync_write.py 94, robotis_def.py 75, packet_handler.py 33 = 1272 lines.
layers.ifMissing: Without sync_write you send 6 separate write packets per tick and pay 6 round trips; without sync_read you cannot build an observation in under ~10 ms. This is the one layer where the remaining work is real and bounded.

layers.name: Protocol 2.0 framing (CRC-16, byte stuffing, packets)
layers.whatItDoes: Builds and parses instruction/status packets, computes the CRC-16/IBM polynomial, escapes the 0xFF 0xFF 0xFD pattern in payloads.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: vendor. Zero of the surveyed projects wrote this themselves. LeRobot imports dynamixel_sdk; ALOHA/Interbotix links DynamixelSDK from C++; ROBOTIS' own ros2_control plugin links it too.
layers.sizeEstimate: Already done — theirs is 288 lines vs the SDK's ~1164 for the equivalent protocol-2 path (the SDK also carries protocol 1.0, bulk read/write and error-string tables they do not need). Their CRC is verified byte-for-byte against three published ROBOTIS example packets, which is the correct acceptance test.
layers.evidence: lerobot pyproject.toml line 179: `dynamixel = ["dynamixel-sdk>=3.7.31,<3.9.0", "lerobot[pyserial-dep]", "lerobot[deepdiff-dep]"]`. lerobot src/lerobot/motors/motors_bus.py lines 193-300 declares PortHandler/PacketHandler/GroupSyncRead/GroupSyncWrite as typing Protocols — i.e. LeRobot models the SDK's API surface but never reimplements it. ROBOTIS' ros2_control plugin (ROBOTIS-GIT/dynamixel_hardware_interface, src/dynamixel/dynamixel.cpp 2527 lines + dynamixel_hardware_interface.cpp 1706 + dynamixel_info.cpp 477 = 4710 lines of C++) also links the SDK rather than reimplementing the protocol.
layers.ifMissing: Nothing — but note this is the layer they chose to build and it is the ONE layer the field universally buys. That is a deliberate trade of about 3-4 days for full visibility, not an oversight.

layers.name: Serial transport (termios, baud, USB latency)
layers.whatItDoes: Opens /dev/ttyACM0 at 1 Mbps, sets raw mode, manages read timeouts and the USB round-trip latency.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: vendor / off-the-shelf. Everyone uses pyserial. The team replaced it with termios to drop the dependency, which is legitimate but puts the USB latency problem on them.
layers.sizeEstimate: Theirs: _RawSerial, ~60 lines inside dxl_raw.py. DynamixelSDK's port_handler.py is 136 lines and does the same job over pyserial.
layers.evidence: DynamixelSDK python/src/dynamixel_sdk/port_handler.py line 27: `LATENCY_TIMER = 16`, used at line 87 in the packet timeout budget: `(tx_time_per_byte * packet_length) + (LATENCY_TIMER * 2.0) + 2.0`. The SDK assumes a 16 ms USB latency timer. The OMX-F bridges the DXL bus through an OpenRB-150 (ROBOTIS hardware doc, ai.robotis.com/omx/hardware_omx.html), which is a USB-CDC device — hence /dev/ttyACM0 rather than the FTDI /dev/ttyUSB0 of a U2D2. INFERRED, not verified: because CDC-ACM has no FTDI latency_timer sysfs knob, the per-transaction USB latency (~1 ms scale) will dominate the 1.55 ms bus-time budget computed above. Measure it before trusting the arithmetic.
layers.ifMissing: Reads time out or the loop silently runs at 10 Hz instead of 25 Hz with no error.

layers.name: Servo firmware (PID, profile generator, limits, shutdown)
layers.whatItDoes: Runs the position PID at ~2 kHz inside each servo, generates the motion profile between goal positions, enforces the EEPROM position/current limits, latches hardware errors and cuts torque on shutdown conditions.
layers.whoNormallyWritesIt: vendor — never yourself, and this is the layer that every project in this survey leans on hardest.
layers.sizeEstimate: 0 lines. What you write is the ~10 register values that configure it.
layers.evidence: THE SHARPEST CONTRAST IN THIS RESEARCH. ALOHA DISABLES the internal profile: tonyzhaozh/aloha config/puppet_modes_left.yaml sets `profile_type: velocity, profile_velocity: 0, profile_acceleration: 0` for both arm and gripper, so Goal_Position is a step and the servo's PID alone tracks a 50 Hz setpoint stream (aloha_scripts/constants.py: DT=0.02; real_env.py:131-134 `set_joint_positions(..., blocking=False)` then `time.sleep(DT)`). ROBOTIS' OMX recipe does the OPPOSITE: Drive_Mode=4 sets bit 2 = "Time-based Profile: Create Profiles based on time steps" (verified in the XL430-W250 e-manual), which changes the UNITS of Profile_Velocity(112) and Profile_Acceleration(108) from rev/min and rev/min^2 to MILLISECONDS — "Sets the time span for the Profile" and "Sets allowed acceleration time of the Profile". So Profile_Velocity=50, Profile_Acceleration=25 means every Goal_Position write kicks off a 50 ms move with a 25 ms acceleration ramp. At the team's dt=0.04 s the next goal arrives while the servo is still 80% through the previous profile — the servo IS the interpolator, continuously. Also relied on and never rebuilt: Min/Max_Position_Limit (EEPROM 48/52) as the real joint limit, Current_Limit (38) + Goal_Current (102) for the current-based-position gripper grasp, and Shutdown (63) + Hardware_Error_Status (70) as the only actual safety interlock.
layers.ifMissing: You would be writing a 2 kHz torque loop on a Jetson over a 1 Mbps half-duplex bus, which is not possible.

keyFindings: LeRobot already ships a driver for this exact robot. huggingface/lerobot src/lerobot/robots/omx_follower/omx_follower.py (231 lines) declares Motor(11,'xl430-w250'), (12,'xl430-w250'), (13,'xl430-w250'), (14,'xl330-m288'), (15,'xl330-m288'), (16,'xl330-m288') — the team's exact ID and model map. Added 2025-12-15 in PR #2614, docstring credits "Woojin Wie and Junha Cha from ROBOTIS (ai.robotis.com)". ROBOTIS wrote a no-ROS direct-serial driver for their own arm and upstreamed it. There is also omx_leader.py (167 lines) and examples/omx/record_grab.py (422 lines).

ROBOTIS published the authoritative register recipe in 40 lines of Python. ROBOTIS-GIT/lerobot branch feature-omx-devel, omx_follower.py lines 166-208. Joint limits in raw ticks: shoulder_lift 830..3129, elbow_flex 1024..3140, wrist_flex 0..4095, wrist_roll 0..4095; shoulder_pan runs in EXTENDED_POSITION (mode 4) with no limit; gripper in CURRENT_BASED_POSITION (mode 5) with Current_Limit=600, Goal_Current=600, Shutdown=21. All motors: Return_Delay_Time=0, Drive_Mode=4, P=1000, I=0, D=1000, Profile_Velocity=50, Profile_Acceleration=25.

The tick-to-radian constant they could not read is a five-column text file. ROBOTIS-GIT/dynamixel_hardware_interface, param/dxl_model/xl430_w250.model: `Present Position  0.0015339807878856412  rad  signed  -3.14159265359`. That is exactly 2*pi/4096, offset -pi, so rad = tick*2*pi/4096 - pi and tick 2048 = 0 rad. The same file gives Present Velocity = 0.0239691227 rad/s per unit. There are 110 such .model files. The 'opaque C++' around it is 4710 lines (dynamixel.cpp 2527, dynamixel_hardware_interface.cpp 1706, dynamixel_info.cpp 477).

Drive_Mode=4 silently changes the units of two registers. Verified in the XL430-W250 e-manual: Drive Mode bit 2 = "Time-based Profile: Create Profiles based on time steps", and in that mode Profile_Velocity(112) means "Sets the time span for the Profile" in 1 ms units and Profile_Acceleration(108) means "allowed acceleration time" in 1 ms. So ROBOTIS' 50/25 is 50 ms move time with a 25 ms ramp, not 50 rev/min. Anyone reading the velocity-based row of the table gets a number that is wrong by a factor of thousands and no error.

The RAM reset is documented behaviour, not a vendor bug, and there is a register that fixes it. XL430-W250 EEPROM is addresses 0-63, RAM is 64-661. Position D/I/P Gain (80/82/84), Profile Acceleration (108), Profile Velocity (112) and Torque Enable (64) are all RAM and revert every power cycle — XL430 defaults P=640 I=0 D=4000; XL330 defaults P=400 I=0 D=0. Both models carry Startup Configuration at EEPROM address 60 (initial 0, range 0-3) whose bit 1 is "On startup, use the backup data to restore the RAM area" (XL330 needs firmware V46+). LeRobot's answer is simpler: call configure() on every connect.

Bypassing ROS is the majority position by a wide margin, and it is now official. LeRobot RFC #4368 (opened 2026-08-07 by alejodosr): LeRobot core does not depend on ROS 2; six community bridges exist with "incompatible approaches" and "No path I could install against current lerobot". lerobot pyproject.toml has zero ROS anywhere — the hardware extras are `dynamixel = ["dynamixel-sdk", "pyserial"]` and `feetech = ["feetech-servo-sdk", "pyserial"]`. Stars as of today: lerobot 27,557 (5,665 forks), openpi 13,853, SO-ARM100 7,487 — versus open_manipulator 663, physical_ai_tools 145, interbotix_ros_core 46, dynamixel_hardware_interface 39.

The policy-facing API is two methods and a flat dict of floats. lerobot src/lerobot/robots/robot.py (211 lines) has 9 abstract members; only get_observation() and send_action() are in the hot loop. send_action takes {'<motor>.pos': float} and returns what was actually sent. Not poses, not trajectories, not a ROS message. ALOHA is the same shape: env.step(action) with 14 absolute joint positions (aloha_scripts/real_env.py:127). UMI is the exception that proves the rule — env.exec_actions(actions[N,7], timestamps[N]) carries absolute wall-clock times because it has a 125 Hz interpolator underneath to consume them.

Rates cluster into two regimes, and the team sits in the low one. Position-servo direct-serial: LeRobot default fps=30.0 (src/lerobot/rollout/configs.py:297), ALOHA DT=0.02 -> 50 Hz, openpi ALOHA max_hz=50. Industrial arm with interpolator: UMI and Diffusion Policy both run the policy at 10 Hz (eval_real.py `--frequency default=10`) with a 125 Hz UR5 loop or 1000 Hz Franka loop underneath; DROID runs Polymetis at 15 Hz. The team's dt=0.04 s is 25 Hz — squarely in the direct-serial regime, where nobody interpolates in software.

LeRobot's entire interpolation layer is 136 lines of linear lerp and it is off by default. src/lerobot/utils/action_interpolator.py, and src/lerobot/rollout/configs.py `interpolation_multiplier: int = 1`. Compare UMI's equivalent: PoseTrajectoryInterpolator 208 lines + RTDEPositionalController 375 lines + shared-memory ring buffer 219 + queue 187 = ~990 lines, because it has a 12.5x rate gap to bridge and the team does not.

LeRobot's entire safety layer is 35 lines and it is ALSO off by default. ensure_safe_goal_position in src/lerobot/robots/utils.py clamps |goal - present| per joint; OmxFollowerConfig sets `max_relative_target: float | dict | None = None`. There is no watchdog, no e-stop, no software joint limit and no velocity limit anywhere in the repo — a regex for watchdog|estop|e_stop|safety over all 1086 files returns zero paths. The real interlocks are the servo's Min/Max_Position_Limit, Current_Limit, Shutdown byte and Hardware_Error_Status.

The relative-anchor design the team chose is the one case LeRobot's default engine refuses to run. src/lerobot/rollout/inference/sync.py lines 36-47, verbatim: cached chunk actions "get reanchored to the *current* robot state and absolute targets drift through the chunk. Relative-action policies are rejected at context-build time today". Only the RTC engine handles them, via a dedicated `reanchor_relative_rtc_prefix` helper plus a stateful RelativeActionsProcessorStep (rtc.py, 602 lines). UMI dodges it by converting to absolute before the chunk reaches the env (eval_real.py:481 get_real_umi_action).

Chunk consumption has exactly three published patterns and everyone picks one. Open-loop replay: act/imitate_episodes.py:248 re-queries every chunk_size steps; openpi ALOHA action_horizon=25 at 50 Hz = 0.5 s blind. Temporal ensembling: act/imitate_episodes.py:250-259, exponential weights with k=0.01 over every chunk that predicted this timestep. Timestamped scheduling with latency compensation: UMI eval_real.py:502-520 plus example/eval_robots_config.yaml, which declares robot_action_latency: 0.1, gripper_action_latency: 0.1, robot_obs_latency: 0.0001, gripper_obs_latency: 0.01 and camera_obs_latency: 0.17. LeRobot's async path uses chunk_size_threshold=0.5 with weighted_average aggregation.

The remaining gap in their own code is precisely sync_write and sync_read. dxl_basics/dxl_raw.py (288 raw / 202 sloc) has crc16, stuff/unstuff, _RawSerial, Bus.send/recv/txrx/ping/read — and no write(), no sync_read(), no sync_write(). Bus arithmetic at 1 Mbps 8N1: sync_write Goal_Position to 6 servos is a 44-byte frame = 440 us with no status packets; sync_read Present_Position is a 20-byte instruction (200 us) plus six 15-byte status packets (900 us) = 1.11 ms at Return_Delay_Time=0, but 4.10 ms at the factory default of 250. Reading 12 registers one at a time across 6 servos costs 21 ms configured and 57 ms at the factory default.

They have already built the one layer the entire field buys, and skipped one they will need. The DynamixelSDK protocol-2 path is protocol2_packet_handler.py 789 + port_handler.py 136 + group_sync_read.py 145 + group_sync_write.py 94 + robotis_def.py 75 + packet_handler.py 33 = 1272 lines; their 288-line replacement covers the framing but not the group ops. Meanwhile LeRobot's wrapper ABOVE the SDK is larger than the SDK: motors_bus.py 1296 + dynamixel.py 264 + tables.py 217 + encoding_utils.py 67 = 1844 lines.

ROBOTIS' own ROS 2 imitation-learning tool is less capable than what the team already wrote. physical_ai_tools/physical_ai_server/data_processing/data_converter.py lines 178-180 publishes JointTrajectory with exactly one JointTrajectoryPoint and no time_from_start — a position setpoint wearing a trajectory costume. Their receding-horizon JointTrajectory publisher was strictly more sophisticated than the vendor's flagship GUI.

Possible model-number mismatch worth checking before first connect. ROBOTIS' hardware page (ai.robotis.com/omx/hardware_omx.html) lists the OMX-F gripper as XL330-M077-T at ID 16, while both upstream LeRobot and the ROBOTIS fork declare Motor(16, 'xl330-m288'). Model numbers differ (M077=1190, M288=1200 in src/lerobot/motors/dynamixel/tables.py), so a strict model check would fail. The team's s1_ping.py will settle it in one run — it is exactly the right first experiment.
tripwires: Nothing in any of these stacks arbitrates the serial port. LeRobot, ALOHA and UMI all assume exactly one process owns the device for the whole session. The teammate's PWM experiment colliding on /dev/ttyACM0 was not a bug they could have diagnosed — it is an unhandled case by design everywhere. Fix it socially (one owner, a lock file, or a udev symlink per person), not in code.

The OMX-F bridges through an OpenRB-150, which is USB-CDC — hence /dev/ttyACM0, not the FTDI /dev/ttyUSB0 that most DYNAMIXEL documentation and every FTDI latency_timer tuning guide assumes. DynamixelSDK's port_handler.py hardcodes LATENCY_TIMER = 16 (ms) into its timeout budget. INFERRED: the per-transaction USB latency will dominate the 1.55 ms of computed bus time. Measure one sync_read round trip with time.perf_counter before designing the loop around the arithmetic.

Their dt = 0.04 s (25 Hz) against ROBOTIS' Profile_Velocity = 50 ms means the servo is still ~20% short of the previous goal when the next one arrives. That is good — it is free smoothing and the reason no software interpolator is needed — but it also means commanded position leads achieved position by roughly one tick, permanently. Any closed-loop comparison of commanded vs present will show a constant lag that is not an error. It will also interact with the 6.48 mm droop measurement: part of that number is profile lag, not gravity.

Drive_Mode is a bitfield, not an enum, and LeRobot's own code treats it as an enum. Upstream omx_follower.calibrate() writes DriveMode.NON_INVERTED (value 0), which CLEARS bit 2 and silently switches the servo back to velocity-based profiles — at which point Profile_Velocity=50 stops meaning 50 ms and starts meaning 50 * 0.229 rev/min. Meanwhile ROBOTIS' shipped calibration JSON (src/lerobot/robots/omx_follower/calibration/omx_follower_arm.json in the fork) has drive_mode: 4 for all six motors. Upstream LeRobot and the ROBOTIS fork disagree about this register. Pick one, write it explicitly on every connect, and read it back.

max_relative_target defaults to None, so LeRobot ships with its only software safety clamp disabled. Worse, enabling it costs a full extra sync_read per tick (omx_follower.py send_action reads Present_Position to compute the clamp), roughly doubling bus time. Decide this deliberately rather than inheriting the default.

shoulder_pan runs in EXTENDED_POSITION mode, where Min/Max_Position_Limit are ignored by firmware. It is the one joint with no hardware limit, and it is the yaw axis their IK derives from atan2(y, x - BASE_X). A bad anchor or a wrapped angle there has nothing stopping it.

Their chunk is anchor-relative, which is exactly the case LeRobot's synchronous engine refuses to run because per-tick re-anchoring makes absolute targets drift through the chunk (sync.py lines 36-47). Take the anchor ONCE when the chunk arrives, expand all 16 steps to absolute immediately, and queue absolute targets. Do not carry the deltas into the queue.

H=16 at dt=0.04 is 0.64 s of open loop — shorter than every library default (ACT 100 steps = 3.3 s at 30 Hz, pi0/SmolVLA 50 steps = 1.0 s at 50 Hz). That is a defensible choice, but it means inference must complete in well under 0.64 s or the queue starves. Instrument the queue depth from day one; LeRobot's async client exposes debug_visualize_queue_size for exactly this reason and re-infers at chunk_size_threshold=0.5.

Reading the control table one register at a time costs 21 ms per full sweep with Return_Delay_Time=0 and 57 ms at the factory default of 250. s2_read.py will feel fine and be entirely misleading about what the control loop can afford. Write Return_Delay_Time=0 to all six servos before you benchmark anything — it is EEPROM, so it persists, unlike the PID gains.

Their s1_ping.py and s2_read.py are the right first two experiments, but there is a third that matters more and does not exist yet: a sync_write of Goal_Position to all six servos, then sync_read of Present_Position, timed in a loop for sixty seconds, logging worst-case tick duration. Everything above the bus is unbuildable until that number is known and stable.

Both LeRobot and ALOHA reboot or explicitly reconfigure the gripper motor on reset (ALOHA calls robot_reboot_motors('single','gripper',True) at the top of every episode; ROBOTIS sets Shutdown=21 on the gripper specifically). A current-based-position gripper that hits its Current_Limit latches a hardware error and drops torque silently. Read Hardware_Error_Status (address 70) every tick or you will spend a day on a gripper that 'randomly stops working'.

There is no watchdog anywhere in this ecosystem. If the Python process dies mid-motion, torque stays enabled and the servo holds its last Goal_Position indefinitely. LeRobot's only mitigation is disable_torque_on_disconnect: True plus a __del__ safety net, which does not fire on SIGKILL. For a 12 V arm near a student's hands, a hardware power switch within reach is the real e-stop.
